chapters.title: The Shipyard
chapters.text:
Almagest Standard Date: Year 1, Day 1
During the early years of Almagest exploration, HEI personnel were granted the time and
resources by the Colonial Authority to pursue a variety of research and development
projects. Many of these initiatives had been planned before humanity’s departure from
Earth, while others emerged during the Almagest mission itself. Ten thousand years is a
long time for research to continue.
Unfortunately, the absence of new data and real-world experimentation meant there was
no miraculous technological revolution waiting on the other side of the journey. Progress
had continued, but mostly in small increments. There had been a handful of major
breakthroughs in specialized fields, but nothing that fundamentally transformed
civilization. One of the projects approved by the Colonial Authority was the
establishment of an independent HEI shipbuilding program. To support this effort, HEI
Shipyards—Almagest Division—was authorized to construct a small orbital shipyard and
begin testing in-house spacecraft production.
HEI still had thousands of specialists sleeping in cryogenic storage, waiting to be
awakened during the next phase of humanity’s expansion.
Among them was Captain James Bell.
James had spent most of his life commanding ships. Now in his mid-fifties, he was a
seasoned officer who had volunteered for the Almagest mission decades earlier. He had
also brought along a trusted crew, all volunteers. His weapons officer was Valencia
Doolittle.
His co-pilot was Jack “Oh Fuck” Daniels.
His senior engineer was Bella Thomas.
And his junior engineer was Marcus “Tropic” Adams.
These were the people James trusted most.


Almagest Standard Date: Year 2, Day 1
James was the first member of his crew to be awakened. As consciousness slowly
returned, he found himself groggy, lightheaded, and weak. Ten thousand years of
cryogenic sleep would do that to a person.
A middle-aged woman approached from the corridor outside his chamber, her heels
clicking against the metal deck as she walked. Still disoriented, James looked around and
realized he was aboard a ship. The woman checked his vitals, nodded with approval, and
simply told him to follow her.
They passed through airlocks and corridors, rode escalators and several vertical lifts, and
eventually arrived on the bridge. For the first time since leaving Earth, James saw the
Almagest system with his own eyes. He stepped toward the forward windows and stared
into the darkness.
There was Verdure.
And there was her moon.
The sight stole his breath.
For several moments he simply stood there in silence. A man in a formal Colonial
Authority uniform eventually approached and gave him a reassuring pat on the shoulder.
“Captain Bell,” the man said. “Welcome to Almagest. I’m Governor Princeton.”
James nodded slowly.
Princeton remembered his own awakening and recognized the distant look in James’s
eyes. Everyone who came out of cryo carried it for a little while. The governor gestured
toward two individuals standing near one of the command consoles.
“This is Captain Ferguson,” he said. “And Vice Admiral Bishop.”
The admiral looked up from his console with a grin.
“How was your nap?”
Still struggling through the haze of cryo recovery, James turned toward him.
Then his eyes widened.
“Daniel?” he asked in disbelief. “When the hell did you get put on the Almagest
mission?”
Bishop laughed.
“Not long after you went to sleep. There was an opening after a casualty, and I decided to
volunteer for the position.”
He crossed his arms.
“I saw your name in the personnel logs years ago, but nobody ever told me why you were
coming out here.”
His grin widened.
“I’m glad to know you’re still taking the fun jobs.”
For the first time since waking, James smiled. In a place as distant and unfamiliar as
Almagest, familiarity was a rare commodity.
Bishop motioned toward the nearby console.
“Take a look.”
Displayed above it was the HEI logo alongside a holographic model of a shipyard.
James studied it carefully.
He knew the original project. It was supposed to be a small manufacturing facility
intended to produce shuttles and light transport craft for the growing colonies.
But this design was different.
Larger.
More capable.
Built to support the construction of medium-sized ships and industrial vehicles.
James looked over at Bishop.
“So everything gets bigger in Almagest?”
His sarcasm was impossible to miss.
Bishop raised an eyebrow.
“You do realize you’re still an officer, right?”
The two men exchanged smirks.
The smirk of two friends who had known each other nearly their entire lives.
James reached out for a handshake.
Instead, Bishop pulled him into a hug.
The two spent the next several hours catching up. Years had passed between James
entering cryo and Bishop boarding the mission.
They had grown up together.
Same neighborhood.
Same schools.
Same college.
Even after their careers had taken them in different directions, they always found time to
return home, visit family, and catch up with one another.
Their friendship ran deep.
Eventually, James was briefed on his assignment. He would command a small freighter
loaded with construction materials, food supplies, industrial equipment, and personnel
needed to establish the new HEI facility.
His team would accompany him.
Approximately fifty engineers and several scientists had already been assigned to the
project.
James made one change.
He kept his personal crew in cryogenic storage.
There was no reason to wake them yet.
He would wait until the station was nearly complete.
One year later, construction of the shipyard had reached approximately fifty percent
completion. Most of the critical systems were already operational. Gravity generators
hummed throughout the station.
Oxygen production was stable.
Solar arrays stretched across several support trusses. Reactor systems provided reliable
baseline power. The facility even included a large recreation dome enclosed by reinforced
glass, offering workers a place to relax while surrounded by the stars.
The shipyard itself was located within the Vedere Belt, roughly three hundred kilometers
from the orbital waystation positioned above Verdure. For the first time since humanity
had arrived in Almagest, HEI was building something entirely its own. ——About a year
into the project, James decided it was finally time to wake his crew.
Year 1, Day 1
They were still young. He had no desire to waste years of their lives on routine
construction work in a distant corner of the galaxy. They had all volunteered for the
mission and understood what they were signing up for, but James was their captain. To
him, they were family.
In many ways, they were his children.
Every one of them.
He would gladly give his life for any member of his crew, and he knew without question
that each of them would do the same for him. One by one, they emerged from cryogenic
sleep. The same fogginess that had greeted James struck each of them just as hard.


The cryo bay was located adjacent to the station’s medical wing along one of the primary
corridors. As each crew member awakened, medical personnel escorted them through a
complete examination to ensure that ten thousand years of sleep had not caused any
complications. Jack, being Jack, managed to cause trouble almost immediately. Still
disoriented and barely awake, he stepped out of his cryo pod, took three unsteady steps,
and promptly fell face-first into the deck.
The impact left a bruise across his forehead that looked suspiciously like the pattern of a
metal floor grate.


There was a moment of silence.
Jack slowly pushed himself up onto his elbows.
“Oh… fuck.”
Without missing a beat, both James and Valencia repeated it.
“Oh, fuck.”
Valencia looked over at James.
“He still doesn’t have his sea legs, apparently. How many gunfights have we been
through, and he still manages to do this?”
James chuckled.
“Hey, we’re still here, right? Things always work out.”
He pointed toward Jack.
“Even when they start with landing face-first into a metal grate.”
The two of them looked back toward their unfortunate co-pilot.
Jack glared at both of them.
“Go fuck yourselves.”

She and Jack were two peas in a pod. They worked side by side, doing almost everything
together.

The attending nurse was far less amused.
They helped Jack back to his feet and she handed him a packet of mild pain medication.
“Try not to fall over anything else.”
Jack looked at her with complete indignation.

Once he was standing again, Valencia gave him a mild punch to the chest to help wake
him up.

It did.

The nurse simply stared back.
She had already decided she didn’t get paid enough for this. A short time later, Jack
finally made his way to the bridge, where James, Valencia, and the rest of the crew had
gathered. Most of them were already awake and recovering in the station galley with
fresh coffee in hand.
The station itself had been designed with a simple philosophy.
If people were going to spend years living and working in deep space, they deserved a
view worth looking at. Large observation windows stretched along the habitation
sections, all carefully positioned to face Verdure.
The planet dominated the sky.
From the station’s location within the asteroid belt, the view was breathtaking. The
asteroids themselves formed a thin cloud of drifting rock and dust that stretched across
the horizon. When morning arrived and the local sun began to rise over Verdure’s distant
curve, the light scattered through the dust field in brilliant shades of gold and amber.
It looked as if the stars themselves were waking up. For several minutes, the crew stood
quietly, staring out the windows.
No one spoke.
Some sights demanded silence.
It had taken humanity only a few thousand people and ten thousand years of travel to
witness this moment. For the first time, many of them truly felt that they had arrived.
***
The crew gathered around a small lunch table in the station galley, talking, laughing, and
catching up on everything they had missed.


At first, they were a little annoyed.
When James explained that he had been awake for nearly a year, they immediately
realized what that meant. The station around them hadn’t appeared overnight.
“You’ve been here a year?” Marcus asked.
James nodded.
“And you didn’t wake us?”
Several members of the crew gave him the same look.
James shrugged.
“Would you rather spend a year doing paperwork and welding in a spacesuit while
boiling your ass off? Or would you rather take a slightly longer nap?”
The table went silent for a moment.
Then everyone started laughing.
They knew James.
They knew he had made the decision for one reason and one reason only: he wanted to
give his crew the best possible start in their new lives. The conversation continued late
into the evening.
Old stories were retold.
Arguments were resumed exactly where they had been left ten thousand years earlier.
Friendships picked up as if no time had passed at all. Their bond had always been
stronger than that of a typical crew.
Most crews went home at the end of the day.
For them, home was each other.
The place they had grown up no longer existed except in memory. Earth was ten thousand
years and an entire galaxy away.
Out here, family was not defined by blood.
It was defined by trust.
Not only had the crew become family, but so had nearly everyone aboard the station.
Life in Almagest demanded it.
Year 1, Day 30
By the second year, things began to get interesting. HEI’s research divisions had
completed studies on a new generation of spacecraft. Ships that would have been largely
unnecessary in the Sol system due to its mature infrastructure.
Almagest was different.
Distances were greater.
Support networks were smaller.
Reliability mattered more than efficiency.
The new vessels emphasized endurance, resilience, power, and presence. Among the first
concepts were the Excalibur Mod 6, the Featherfall Freighter, the Outlander Industrial
Platform, and the Borehole Miner. After attending a joint presentation by Colonial
Authority officials and HEI management, James finally understood why the shipyard had
been built larger than originally planned.
HEI had been given a much greater role in the development of the system. The early
years of colonization had been difficult.
Ships constantly required repair.
Components intended for completely different purposes had been bolted together simply
because there were no alternatives. Entire vessels were assembled from salvaged parts,
recycled equipment, and whatever materials happened to be available at the time. Many
looked as though they might fall apart at any moment.
Yet they continued operating because they had to. Humanity did not have the luxury of
waiting. Recognizing the growing need for reliable transportation and industrial
infrastructure, HEI Shipyards—Almagest Division—began expanding beyond simple
maintenance work.
Almagest Standard Date: Year 2, Day 1
The company took on a larger role in shipbuilding, manufacturing, and large-scale
retrofitting. Initially, the station spent most of its time repairing and modifying existing
hulls. Old colony support vessels were strengthened.
Cargo ships were upgraded.
Frames designed for one task were adapted to perform another.
Over time, HEI became known for this work.
If a ship needed to travel farther, carry more, survive longer, or simply stop breaking
down every few weeks, HEI was the company people called. The quality of their work
did not go unnoticed. As confidence in the company grew, the Colonial Authority
provided additional resources, personnel, and manufacturing contracts.
Behind the scenes, much of the groundwork had already been completed. The AI
research divisions aboard the Almagest colony fleet had spent ten thousand years
processing engineering models. Millions of hull configurations had been analyzed.
Structural designs had been optimized.
Life-support systems had been refined.
Advances in manufacturing, materials science, spacesuit technology, and industrial
engineering had accumulated over centuries of uninterrupted computation. Now, for the
first time, those designs could become reality. The first vessel to roll off the line was the
new Expedition Shuttle.
Though still classified as a shuttle, it possessed far greater range and capability than any
small craft previously operating within Almagest.
Next came the Featherfall Freighter.
Then the Outlander Industrial Platform.
Then the Borehole Miner.
The shipyard itself was not particularly large. Its production capacity was modest
compared to the great orbital shipyards humanity had once imagined. But the ships it
produced became the backbone of a growing civilization.
They hauled cargo.
They transported settlers.
They built stations.
They mined resources.
They connected distant communities across the system. They represented the beginning
of a future. The foundation upon which a civilization would be built.
HEI was not alone in this effort.
Many companies, organizations, and government agencies were contributing in their own
ways. Throughout Almagest, shipyards were being assembled, industries were forming,
and new settlements were taking root. Humanity was finally beginning to spread its
wings.
But James Bell was a captain.
A captain of HEI.
And a captain within the Colonial Authority. The story he cared about was the one
unfolding directly in front of him.
***
There was one project that remained unfinished. One ship that had yet to leave the
drawing board.
Excalibur.
The real reason James Bell had been brought to Almagest. The real reason he had
assembled the crew he did. James was never an engineer. He did not oversee
manufacturing schedules, structural design studies, reactor layouts, or propulsion testing.
That was someone else’s job.
His responsibility was much simpler.
He was going to fly it.
More importantly, he was going to be the first person to fly it.
James Bell had been selected as the lead test captain for the Excalibur Program, and his
crew would become some of the first people to carry humanity beyond the established
settlements of Almagest.
They would chart routes.
Test systems.
Survey distant regions.
And discover what existed beyond the frontier. The Excalibur Program had begun as a
series of experimental corvette designs intended to create a ship capable of operating
independently for extended periods far from support infrastructure. Early prototypes had
shown promise, but they also revealed significant limitations.
The most famous of these early vessels was the Excalibur Mod 6. To say it was imperfect
would have been generous.
It was ugly.
The hull proportions were awkward.
Maintenance access was difficult.
Several engineers privately described it as “a collection of compromises wrapped around
a railgun.” Yet despite its flaws, the ship possessed one remarkable characteristic. The
hull had been engineered far beyond what most considered reasonable.
Somehow, the designers had managed to fit an XR-9 Godspear Railgun onto a vessel
measuring only seventy-three meters in length, thirty-five meters in width, and fifteen
meters in height. For a corvette, it was an astonishing achievement. The Mod 6 was
followed by additional revisions as engineers continued refining the concept.
Each version corrected flaws discovered in testing while improving reliability,
survivability, and long-range capability. The lessons learned from those early ships would
ultimately lead to something much more ambitious.
For eighteen months, engineers, researchers, and manufacturing specialists worked
around the clock. The Colonial Authority continued providing resources.
HEI continued expanding its facilities.
And the Excalibur team continued pushing the limits of what a small independent
spacecraft could be. The result was the first production example of an entirely new frame.
The HEI Excalibur-class Star Chaser 1-M R-1.0.
Unlike the earlier Excalibur variants, the 1-M was not simply another modification. It
was a fundamentally redesigned vessel built from the ground up using everything the
company had learned during the development of the original program. Long-range
operations were no longer an afterthought.
They were the mission.
The ship incorporated improved habitation facilities, expanded cargo capacity, enhanced
systems redundancy, stronger structural protection, and the ability to operate
independently for extended periods without external support. Most importantly, it
remained unmistakably an Excalibur.
Fast.
Heavily armed for its size.
Built to survive.
Built to explore.
Built to keep going when other ships would turn around. As James stood inside the
construction hangar and looked up at the completed vessel for the first time, he felt
something he had not experienced in years.
Pride.
Not because he had designed it.
Not because he had built it.
But because he had watched it become real.
The ship represented more than another contract or another production run. It represented
the future of HEI in Almagest. It represented the future of long-range exploration.
And in only a few short hours, James Bell and his crew would become the first people to
put it to the test.
Every reactor online.
Every thruster active.
Every system operational.
Every weapon armed.
Year 3, Day 182
For the first time, the Excalibur was ready to fly. And James Bell intended to take her
farther than anyone had ever gone before. —The crew stood together in the hangar,
staring upward.
Excalibur dominated the bay.
She was massive.


A brutal, angular hammerhead shape that somehow still managed to look sleek and
elegant. Her armor plates flowed together in sharp lines and purposeful geometry, every
surface designed around function rather than appearance. The broad forward hull
projected confidence, while the long body stretching behind it hinted at endurance and
self-sufficiency. Beneath the ship sat the feature that had defined the entire program.
The XR-9 Godspear.
Its armored housing ran along the lower centerline of the vessel, recessed into the belly
and protected by layers of structure and armor. Even sitting idle, it felt imposing.
Around them, the ship hummed with life.
Power conduits carried energy throughout the vessel.
Cooling systems cycled.
Pumps moved fluids through hundreds of meters of piping. Deep within the armored
heart of the ship, eight reactors worked together as a single system. The vibration could
be felt through the deck plating.
It was subtle.
Constant.
Alive.
Eight reactors.
One purpose.
Fire the railgun as many times as possible.
As fast as possible.
For as long as possible.
James smiled.
That was exactly the kind of engineering philosophy he appreciated.
He began walking around the ship.
The landing gear immediately caught his attention.
They were enormous.
Large square footpads supported by thick hydraulic assemblies and reinforced structural
members. The feet themselves did not retract fully into the hull. Instead, they folded into
heavily armored housings where portions remained exposed.
It was not elegant.
It was practical.
Excalibur was heavy.
Far heavier than a ship of her size had any right to be. She was a vessel that should not
have been capable of landing on planets. She was a vessel that should not have been
capable of carrying an XR-9 Godspear.
And yet she did both.
That was the entire point.
Along either side of the hangar, the boarding ramps extended from the ship. Excalibur
boarded horizontally through the rear-center section of the hull.
The ramps led directly into Main Commons.
For many aboard the vessel, Main Commons would become the true heart of the ship.
Two airlocks flanked the room.
A galley and kitchen occupied the center.
To starboard sat the Combat Information Center, protected behind armored partitions.
Running forward from the center of the room was the primary corridor, a spine that
connected nearly every major compartment aboard the ship.
Directly ahead lay the reactor citadel.
Behind reinforced bulkheads to port was the secondary oxygen generation facility. To
starboard stood the ship’s main stairwell and lift shaft, extending vertically through
multiple decks and serving as the primary route between the vessel’s major
compartments. Above were the bridge and crew accommodations.
Below were cargo spaces, maintenance accessways, and support systems. The entire
layout had been designed around one simple requirement: No matter what happened, the
crew needed a way to reach critical systems.
Eventually the engineers gave their approval.
The ship was theirs.
At least for today.
The vessel had already undergone extensive dockside testing.
Reactors had been brought online.
Thrusters had been fired under restraint.
Life-support systems had been validated.
Power systems had been stress-tested.
The ship could function.
Everyone knew that.
The real test was still ahead.
Charging the XR-9.
Firing the XR-9.
Charging the jump drive.
And performing the vessel’s first jump.
Back in Sol, such tests would have involved committees, oversight boards, review panels,
and enough paperwork to fill an entire cargo container.
In Almagest?
People were mostly figuring things out as they went. James performed one final walk
around the exterior.
He inspected weld seams.
Checked armor joints.
Examined thruster housings.
Looked for signs of leakage around fuel systems and service ports.
Everything looked pristine.
The engineers had done exceptional work.
Finally, the crew boarded.
They entered through the airlock and stepped into Main Commons. From there they
moved methodically throughout the ship.
They inspected the reactor room.
Checked access panels.
Verified emergency systems.
Reviewed oxygen and environmental controls.
Hangar mechanisms were tested.
Shuttle launch systems were cycled.
Airlock seals were inspected.
Backup systems were activated.

In engineering, Bella Thomas carefully reviewed the secondary reactor startup sequence.
The auxiliary reactor came online exactly as expected.

Marcus "Tropic" Adams worked beside her.

Marcus was nineteen, but towered over everyone. He was a six-foot-five Black man with
a mohawk and tattoos to match, and he knew it. His nickname, "Tropic," came from his
love of an old Earth movie, Tropic Thunder, the only movie he had ever bothered to bring
with him. He had a soft face that didn't match his size, though.

A gentle giant.

He had spent the first two years of adulthood making mistakes that couldn't be taken
back, and somehow convinced James Bell to drag him ten thousand years from Earth to
escape a past that had caught up with him far too quickly.

James never asked Marcus to explain it.

He simply handed him a wrench and told him to start building something worth a damn.
Now Marcus spent nearly an hour checking power-routing systems and environmental
controls before finally declaring himself satisfied.

Eventually, the crew made their way upward.
To the bridge.
They had all seen it before.
Most of them had walked through it while construction crews were still installing
bulkheads. Some had visited while engineers were still laying wiring beneath the deck.
But now it was finished.
Now it was real.
This was their ship.
Their home.
Their responsibility.
Each member of the crew moved toward their station.
Valencia inspected the weapons consoles.
Jack examined the flight controls.
Bella reviewed engineering telemetry.
Marcus checked environmental and support systems along with the sensor networks,
Bella watched closely.
For several moments nobody spoke.
They simply sat there.
Admiring the result of eighteen months of effort.
The bridge itself was spacious.
Forward observation windows stretched across the front of the compartment, offering a
breathtaking view of Verdure and the surrounding asteroid belt. The command stations
formed a semicircle around the captain’s chair.
Behind them sat a briefing table.
Unlike the sterile conference rooms common aboard government vessels, this one felt
almost personal. The crew could gather there for mission planning.
Meals.
Paperwork.
Arguments.
Celebrations.
Or simply to sit together and watch Almagest drift by beyond the glass.
James stood quietly in front of his chair.
Then he turned toward his crew.
Jack Daniels.
Valencia Doolittle.
Bella Thomas.
Marcus Adams.
His family.
“I just wanted to say thank you.”
The room grew quiet.
“You didn’t have to come out here.”
Nobody interrupted.
“You didn’t have to volunteer. You didn’t have to leave everything behind. You sure as
hell didn’t have to follow me across ten thousand years and another galaxy.”
A few smiles appeared around the room.
“But you did.”
James paused.
Looking at each of them.
“Every one of you helped get us here.”
He pointed toward the deck beneath his feet.
“This ship exists because thousands of people worked on her.”
Then he pointed around the bridge.
“But we’re the ones who get to fly her.”
Jack grinned.
“Damn right.”
A few laughs followed.

James smiled.

Over the last eighteen months, every member of the crew had found ways to contribute.
James had assisted station operations and Colonial Authority logistics.

Jack had spent countless hours flying supply runs throughout the belt.

Bella had worked alongside construction teams and reactor specialists.

Marcus had assisted Bella with environmental systems, fabrication projects, and station
maintenance, learning from her every chance he got.

Valencia had helped develop training programs, working with station personnel on
hand-to-hand combat, safety procedures, and weapons integration testing. Jack usually
volunteered to help, while Bella and Marcus often tagged along. Whether they were there
to learn something new or simply because they enjoyed giving each other a hard time,
nobody was ever quite sure.

They had all earned their place here.

Looking around the bridge, James found himself reflecting on the decision he had made
eighteen months earlier. Maybe he should have left them in cryo a little longer.

The thought lasted all of two seconds.
No.
This was where they belonged.
Together.
Exactly where they were supposed to be.
***
Through the intercom, James heard a familiar voice.
Bishop.
Apparently, the admiral had taken the time to travel all the way across his corner of the
system just to personally see Excalibur depart. James looked through the bridge windows
toward the observation deck attached to the station. At that angle, the triple-layer armored
glass made it difficult to see clearly. Reflections danced across the surface. The viewing
panels had never been intended to be observed from the side.
​


Daniel Bishop and James Bell had grown up together.

The same block.
The same town.

They went to the same schools, played on the same football team, attended the same
college, and even enlisted in the Navy together.

That was where the Navy decided to separate them.

The Navy did that.

Friends, brothers, husbands and wives—it didn't matter. The service had learned long ago
that the battlefield had a way of making people choose each other over the mission.
Separating lifelong friends made those decisions easier.

It never changed anything between James and Daniel.

Whenever they found themselves back on Earth at the same time, they always managed
to catch up over a drink, spend time with their families, and complain about whatever the
Navy had managed to screw up that year.

Ten thousand years and another galaxy hadn't changed that either.

Part of the distortion came from the smart filtering system embedded within the glass
itself. The software constantly adjusted transparency and polarization to prevent the crew
from being blinded when looking toward the local star. It was a small price to pay for a
bridge wrapped in windows. Through the reflections, James could just make out Bishop.
The admiral raised a hand.
Then he saluted.
A moment later the intercom clicked again.
“You ladies and gentlemen are good to go.”
There was a brief pause.
“Say hello to the engineers at Kemik Station for me.”
The transmission ended.
James smiled.
Then he turned toward the bridge crew.

Immediately the bridge came alive.

Jack Daniels slid into the center command console while Valencia Doolittle settled into
the weapons station to port. Marcus “Tropic” Adams occupied the systems console to
starboard.
The center chair technically belonged to James.

It was the captain’s station.

His station.

But James had no intention of sitting today.

Not on the first flight.

Not on the maiden voyage.

Instead, he reached up, grabbed one of the overhead handrails running along the ceiling,
and positioned himself behind the crew where he could watch everything unfold.

Beside him, Bella Thomas did the same.

The senior engineer folded her arms and leaned casually against one of the support
pillars. She looked entirely too relaxed for someone standing aboard a brand-new
corvette moments before its first flight.

“If this thing explodes,” she said, “I’m blaming every engineer except me.”

James laughed.

“That’s fair.”

Marcus rolled his eyes from his console.

“Good to know where the chain of command stands.”

Bella smirked.

“You’ll understand when you’re older.”

Marcus immediately looked offended.

Bella enjoyed that far more than she should have.

Despite the joking, both engineers had already reviewed the ship extensively. Every
major system had been checked and rechecked. Thousands of diagnostic routines had
been completed.

Now it was time to trust the machine.
Marcus began working through the final system verification.

“Primary reactors stable.”

“Power distribution nominal.”

“Environmental systems green.”

“Hydrogen systems green.”

“Communications green.”

One by one the reports came in.

Valencia confirmed weapons safeties and targeting systems.

Jack verified flight controls and propulsion systems.

The bridge gradually grew quiet.

The last checklists disappeared from the displays.

The final diagnostics completed.

The waiting was over.

Everyone looked toward James.

One by one, they raised a thumb.

“Green light.”

“Green light.”

“Green light.”

James turned his head slightly toward Bella.

For a moment she studied the engineering telemetry scrolling across her portable display.
Then she nodded once.

“She’s ready.”

That was all he needed to hear.
Standing beside him, Bella rested one hand on the rail and looked out through the bridge
windows at the stars beyond the shipyard. James followed her gaze.

Eighteen months of construction.

Thousands of workers.

thousands of hours.

Every weld.

Every cable.

Every reactor component.

Every armor plate.

All of it had led to this moment.

Neither of them said anything.

They didn't need to.

Excalibur was ready to fly.


Deep within the hull, the twin oversized main thrusters began their startup sequence.
At first there was only a low vibration.
A distant hum.
Then the vibration intensified.
The deck trembled beneath their feet.
The sound built steadily into a deep mechanical roar.
The engines felt alive.
Like a caged beast straining against its restraints. Like a bull trapped inside a china shop
with nowhere to run.
The ship wanted to move.
Every vibration seemed to communicate the same thing.
Let me go.
Secondary maneuvering thrusters activated next. Small attitude corrections rippled
through the vessel.
Docking restraints disengaged.
Across the hangar, warning lights flashed.
Gravity generators inside the bay powered down.
The massive hangar doors began to open.
Hydraulic systems groaned.
Warning klaxons echoed through the station. Excalibur’s landing gear started to retract.
The enormous hydraulic assemblies folded upward into their armored housings.
Metal scraped against metal.
Actuators rotated.
Locking pins engaged.
Then came the final sound.
A deep, reassuring hissing and then a deep clunk.
The kind of sound that told every engineer aboard the ship that something heavy had just
locked exactly where it was supposed to.
Bella smiled.
Marcus nodded approvingly.
Even James found himself grinning.
Everything was working.
Every system.
Every weld.
Every component.
Eighteen months of work.
Thousands of people.
Millions of hours.
All leading to this moment.
For the first time, the HEI Excalibur-class Star Chaser 1-M R-1.0 was ready to leave the
shipyard.
Ready to leave home.
Ready to prove herself.
***
Immediately the bridge came alive.
***
Excalibur slowly drifted away from the shipyard. The twin oversized main thrusters
remained dormant. They were simply too powerful to use in such close proximity to the
station. A full-power burn would have flooded the surrounding area with plasma and
done enough to catastrophically damage nearby structures.
Instead, the ship relied on its secondary maneuvering thrusters.
Their purpose was simple.
Precision.
Station keeping.
Docking.
Long-duration corrections over vast distances. The smaller thrusters carefully guided
Excalibur clear of the station.
Slowly.
Deliberately.
For the first time in her existence, she floated freely in space.
The bridge remained quiet.
Everyone understood the significance of the moment. The ship rotated ninety degrees
away from the station. Beyond the bridge windows, the shipyard hung against the stars.
Observation decks and command centers were packed with spectators.
Engineers.
Scientists.
Colonial Authority officials.
Shipyard workers.
Nearly everyone who had contributed to the project had found a window somewhere.
Among them stood Admiral Bishop.
Watching.
Smiling.
Grinning ear to ear.
This was the moment they had all been waiting for.
The reason the ship existed.
The reason it carried the name Excalibur.
Marcus glanced over from his console.
“We’re ready.”
Bella looked at him and nodded.
A small grin crossed her face.
Marcus switched channels.
“Reactors one through eight coming online for weapons testing.”
Five seconds passed.
The vibration began immediately.
Deep within the ship, power systems rerouted energy toward the XR-9 Godspear.
The hum of the reactors intensified.
The deck plates vibrated beneath their feet.
Valencia looked over her shoulder.
Her grin grew wider.
“Looks real good.”
Standing behind the crew, James and Bella watched the system readouts. Bella’s eyes
constantly moved between the displays and James. Whenever he checked a value, she
checked it too.
Years of working together had made the process instinctive.
Neither trusted first-run data.
Not today.
Not on this ship.
Not on this weapon.
Everything looked perfect.
James looked toward Valencia.
“Fire at test target one.”
Valencia nodded.
The targeting controls transferred to her station. One of Excalibur’s unique features
allowed the weapons officer to assume limited control of the ship’s orientation during
firing sequences. Rather than forcing the pilot to constantly maneuver for weapons
alignment, the targeting system could rotate the vessel several degrees independently,
allowing precise adjustments for firing solutions.
Jack glanced toward her.
“You have the controls?”
Valencia placed her hands on the targeting interface.
“I have the controls.”
In combat, the exchange would have taken less than a second.
Today was different.
Nobody was rushing anything.
The ship was robust.
The engineering was sound.
But they didn’t know her yet.
Valencia began the charging sequence.
The XR-9 Godspear came alive.
A low electrical buzz spread through the hull.
Capacitor banks charged.
Power conduits glowed.
The hum grew louder.
Then louder still.
The entire ship seemed to tense.
Waiting.
Valencia smiled.
“Railgun charged.”
James nodded.
“Fire.”
The XR-9 discharged.
A brilliant flash mixed with metal sparks and superheated plasma erupted beneath the
ship and extended 50 meters in front of the barrel.
The bridge shook.
A violent crack echoed through the hull.
The recoil slammed backward into the ship’s structure. Almost instantly the rear thruster
banks roared to life, fighting to counteract the force.
The entire vessel shuddered.
Then silence.
Everyone stared at the targeting display.
Five kilometers away, the test target vanished.
Direct hit.
The round had impacted less than a foot from the designated center point.
Nobody spoke for a moment.
Then the bridge erupted into cheers.
The first test was complete.
James grinned.
“That felt good.”
Valencia laughed.
“Little bit.”
James pointed toward the next marker.
“Go ahead and wrap up tests two and three.”
Valencia aligned Excalibur toward the second target.
Ten kilometers.
The XR-9 fired again.
Direct hit.
Twenty kilometers.
Another shot.
Direct hit.
The railgun performed flawlessly.
Over the intercom, someone forgot to release the transmit button.
The bridge suddenly filled with cheering from the shitpyard.
Applause.
Shouting.
Celebration.
The engineers aboard the station were losing their minds.
They had done it.
They had accomplished what many thought impossible.
They had built Excalibur.
Eventually Bishop’s voice cut through the noise. The admiral must have realized the
channel was still open because several seconds of celebration abruptly stopped.
A throat cleared.
Then Bishop spoke.
“All right.”
A pause.
“Time for the real test.”
The bridge grew quiet.
Bishop continued.
“Let’s see what that jump drive can do.”
The XR-9 powered down.
The vibrations throughout the ship gradually faded.
The reactor load shifted.
Capacitors discharged.
The deep hum that had filled the vessel disappeared.
Jack looked toward James.
James simply nodded.
“Punch it.”
Jack smiled.
“Gladly.”
The jump drive began charging.
All eight reactors surged to maximum output. The lights throughout the ship dimmed
slightly as enormous amounts of energy flowed into the drive core. Outside the vessel,
space itself began to distort.
Stars stretched.
Light bent.
Reality seemed to ripple around the ship.
The bridge fell silent.
Nobody moved.
Nobody breathed.
A shimmering fracture appeared ahead of Excalibur. For a brief instant, it looked as
though space and time themselves had folded inward.
Then—
Excalibur vanished.
Gone.
No flash.
No explosion.
No trail.
One moment she was there.
The next she was not.
And with that, the first voyage of the HEI Excalibur-class Star Chaser 1-M R-1.0 had
begun.
***
What happened next would put the Colonial Authority on notice.
Notice of what exactly?
At the time, nobody knew.
Excalibur emerged from the jump violently.
The entire ship jolted.
Metal screamed.
Structural members groaned.
Somewhere deep inside the hull, something sounded as though it had bent beyond its
limits. The bridge shook so hard several crew members were thrown from their feet.
the ship was tumbling.
Power failed almost instantly.
Main reactors offline.
Primary systems offline.
Gravity offline.
Navigation offline.
The only thing still functioning reliably was the atmospheric system. Emergency lighting
flooded the ship in red.
Alarms erupted from every console.
Outside the bridge windows, stars spun wildly. Between flashes of darkness and reflected
light, a massive metallic object repeatedly swept across their field of view as the ship
rotated uncontrollably.
Marcus was already moving.
His hands flew across dead consoles, trying desperately to restore power.
“Bella!”
He didn’t need to say anything else.
Bella was already gone.
The senior engineer sprinted from the bridge.
Down the stairs.
Through the corridors.
Into engineering.
The emergency reactor controls were mounted on a reinforced bulkhead beside the main
power systems. She slammed her hand onto the activation switch.
“Come on.”
Nothing.
She hit it again.
The reactor roared to life.
A moment later emergency power surged throughout the ship.
Systems began rebooting.
Thrusters regained partial control.
The tumbling slowed.
Then stopped.
One by one, critical functions began returning.
But something was wrong.
Very wrong.
The sensors were behaving erratically.
Threat warnings appeared and disappeared.
Targeting systems attempted to initialize.
Then failed.
Then initialized again.
The ship’s computers seemed almost frantic. On the bridge, most of the crew were still
recovering from the violent transition.
Valencia was not.
Jack wasn’t either.
Both had spent years flying vessels that were smaller, faster, and far less forgiving than
Excalibur.
Both looked through the forward windows.
Both saw the same thing.
Both spoke at exactly the same time.
“Oh, fuck.”
The automated combat systems suddenly came alive.
The bridge lighting shifted.
Red alert indicators illuminated throughout the ship. The XR-9 Godspear began charging
automatically.
Point-defense ammunition feeds activated.
Targeting systems initialized.
Missile warning systems armed.
Thrusters entered combat readiness.
The ship’s computer had reached a conclusion before the crew had.
Something was out there.
Something dangerous.
Fuel pressure increased.
Capacitors charged.
Weapons armed.
The entire ship prepared for combat.
And nobody knew why.
Bella finally burst back onto the bridge.
James was still trying to make sense of the sensor data scrolling across the displays.
She stepped beside him.
Looked through the windows.
Then froze.
“What the fuck is that?”
Nobody answered.
Nobody could.
Ahead of them drifted a vessel.
If it could even be called a vessel.
It was enormous.
Its shape flowed unlike anything humanity had ever constructed.
There were no obvious armor plates.
No visible decks.
No recognizable superstructure.
The surface appeared metallic, yet somehow fluid.
As if the object had been grown instead of manufactured.
It was alien.
Completely.
Unequivocally.
Alien.
The possibility had always existed.
The Colonial Authority had contingency plans.
Scientific studies.
Entire departments dedicated to the question.
What if humanity wasn’t alone?
Yet after arriving in Almagest, nothing had ever appeared.
No ruins.
No signals.
No evidence.
Eventually most people stopped thinking about it. Many assumed intelligent alien life
simply didn’t exist.
That humanity was alone.
The stories became background noise.
Interesting theories.
Nothing more.
Not now.
Not this.
James stared through the glass.
His voice was quiet.
Almost trembling.
A tone none of the crew had ever heard from him before.
“Not now.”
The alien vessel continued drifting ahead of them.
Massive.
Silent.
Ancient-looking.
Then sections of its hull began to move.
Hundreds of panels opened.
Then hundreds more.
The bridge suddenly filled with targeting returns.
Valencia’s eyes widened.
She leaned toward her display.
Her voice dropped.
Those weren’t sensor anomalies.
Those weren’t maintenance hatches.
Those weren’t antennas.
They were weapons.
An unbelievable number of weapons.
Valencia looked up slowly.
“Those are guns.”
Nobody spoke.
She swallowed.
Then looked back at the tactical display.
“Lots of guns.”
Another panel opened.
Then another.
Then dozens more.
Valencia stared at the growing wall of threat indicators.
“Lots of really big guns.”
And for the first time since leaving Earth ten thousand years earlier, humanity was no
longer alone. —Bella practically threw herself into the engineering station. Streams of
data were pouring in faster than anyone could process them.
She began sorting, filtering, and pushing the most important information onto the central
holographic display where the entire bridge could see it. At first she thought the sensors
were malfunctioning. Then she thought the calibration tables were corrupted.
Then she realized neither was true.
The readings were real.
Her face slowly lost color.
“James…”
Nobody answered.
Everyone was staring at the display.
Power output.
Reactor signatures.
Energy storage systems.
Thermal emissions.
The numbers continued climbing.
And climbing.
And climbing.
The scales kept automatically expanding to compensate.
Still the readings exceeded them.
Bella zoomed out again.
And again.
And again.
Finally she looked up.
Her voice was barely above a whisper.
“That’s impossible.”
James turned toward her.
Bella pointed at the display.
“Power.”
The single word hung in the air.
“So much power.”
The readings updated again.
Higher.
The display struggled to represent the values.
“We’ve never seen anything like this.”
Nobody spoke.
Bella continued staring at the numbers.
“Even the largest facilities back in Sol couldn’t produce this much energy.”
Another update.
Higher again.
The readout eventually stopped increasing.
Not because the alien vessel had stopped producing power. The sensors had simply
reached their maximum measurable value.
The bridge grew silent.
Nobody wanted to be the first person to say what everyone was thinking. Whatever was
in front of them was operating on an entirely different technological level.
Then something happened.
Nothing.
The alien vessel did not fire.
It did not move.
It did not advance.
It simply remained there.
Watching.
The weapons remained deployed.
The impossible energy readings remained constant.
And yet nothing happened.
James stared through the forward windows.
The alien ship had responded the moment Excalibur armed itself.
Not before.
Not after.
The realization hit him immediately.
He looked toward Valencia.
Then toward Marcus.
His voice was quiet.
Almost a whisper.
“Power down weapons.”
Nobody argued.
Valencia immediately disengaged the XR-9 charging sequence. Marcus began reducing
combat power allocation. The bridge lighting shifted from deep red toward normal
operating conditions.
Throughout the ship, systems began standing down. The roar of the reactors slowly
diminished.
The hum of charged capacitors faded.
Point-defense systems returned to safe status.
Targeting systems disengaged.
The tension aboard Excalibur eased.
A little.
Ten seconds passed.
It felt like hours.
Nobody moved.
Nobody blinked.
Nobody breathed.
Then the alien vessel responded.
One by one, the weapon ports began to close.
Hundreds of panels folded inward.
The guns disappeared back into the flowing metallic hull. Massive weapon systems
vanished behind seamless armor.
Sections of the ship shifted and reformed.
Within moments it looked as though the weapons had never existed at all.
The bridge remained silent.
Everyone understood exactly what had happened. The alien vessel had seen Excalibur
arm itself.
And it had armed itself in return.
Excalibur had stood down.
And so had the alien ship.
James slowly exhaled.
The crew followed a moment later.
Nobody said it aloud.
Nobody needed to.
For the first time in history, humanity had just communicated with an alien civilization.
Without a single word.
And somehow, against all odds, neither side had opened fire.
***
Then, in an instant, the alien vessel was gone.
No flash.
No acceleration.
No visible drive signature.
It simply ceased to exist.
One moment it occupied half the forward view. The next moment there was nothing but
stars.
Silence settled over the bridge.
Nobody moved.
Nobody spoke.
Nobody seemed entirely convinced that what they had just witnessed was real.
James stood quietly for several seconds.
Then he walked toward the main console.
Slowly.
Deliberately.
Like sudden movements might somehow attract attention. Without saying a word, he
began shutting systems down.
Combat systems to standby.
Targeting systems offline.
Sensors to passive mode.
Reactor output reduced.
Eventually only essential systems remained active.
Emergency-power levels.
The bridge grew noticeably quieter.
Still nobody moved.
James turned and walked toward the rear of the bridge. In the back corner sat a small
galley unit.
A refrigerator.
Several storage compartments.
And one cabinet.
James opened it.
Inside was a bottle of whiskey.
Expensive whiskey.
Earth whiskey.
The real thing.
He had carried it all the way from Earth.
Saved it for years.
He had planned to open it after the completion of Excalibur’s maiden voyage.
After a successful first mission.
After everything went according to plan.
Instead, humanity had encountered a technologically superior alien civilization during
Excalibur's first jump.
Close enough.
Nobody stopped him.
In between where Bella and James were standing in the center of the bridge was a small
deployable table recessed into the deck.
James pressed a control panel on an adjacent support pillar.
The circular pedestal rose smoothly from the floor. Embedded within its center was a
cylindrical dispenser.
He pressed another button on the top center of the cylinder that was about 6 inches in
diameter and flush with the table.
The dispenser extended upward.
Six shot glasses unfolded from within.
The bridge remained completely silent.
Finally Jack slowly turned around in his chair.
He stared at the table.
Then at the whiskey.
Then at James.
“Yep.”
A pause.
“That’s what we’re doing now.”
Valencia nodded immediately.
“Absolutely.”
Bella pointed at the bottle.
“Pour me one too.”
Marcus was already standing.
Nobody bothered arguing.
One by one they gathered around the table.
Slowly.
Methodically.
Like people walking through a nightmare.
Nobody quite knew what to say.
Nobody understood what had happened.
They had met aliens.
Actual aliens.
Not microbes.
Not ruins.
Not signals.
Not theories.
Aliens.
And they had apparently survived.
James poured the drinks.
The crew raised their glasses.
Nobody offered a toast.
Nobody could think of one.
They simply drank.
Then they drank another.
The silence continued.
And then—
CLANG.
Every head snapped toward the front of the ship in sheer horror.
A metallic impact echoed through the hull.
Something had attached itself directly ahead of the bridge. The sensors immediately
highlighted the object.
A small contact.
Approximately five feet long.
Half capsule.
Half cylinder.
Smooth.
Featureless.
Attached directly to Excalibur’s hull.
Nobody moved.
Jack stared at the display.
Then looked at the rest of the crew.
“Oh.”
He sighed.
“Here we go again.”
Before anyone could react, space distorted.
The stars stretched.
Reality folded.
And Excalibur jumped.
Not using its own jump drive.
The ship’s systems showed no activation.
No charge sequence.
No reactor demand.
No jump-drive initiation.
The little object attached to the hull had somehow jumped the entire ship.
Instantly.
Without permission.
Without warning.
Without effort.
The bridge remained silent.
Nobody even bothered getting into their seats.
At this point they were simply along for the ride.
Moments later normal space returned.
The navigation systems updated.
Kemik Station.
They were at Kemik.
For a brief moment, nobody on the bridge moved. Then Marcus pointed toward the
forward display.
“The thing is still attached.”
Everyone looked.
The small capsule-shaped object remained fixed to Excalibur’s hull just ahead of the
bridge. As if it had accompanied them the entire journey.
Nobody particularly liked that idea.
Then the object detached.
No mechanical arms.
No visible clamps.
No release sequence.
It simply drifted away from the hull.
Slowly at first.
Almost cautiously.
The crew watched in silence.
The object rotated once, orienting itself away from Excalibur.
Then something strange happened.
A familiar distortion appeared in front of it. Not the impossible folding of reality they had
witnessed near the alien vessel.
This looked different.
Cruder.
More recognizable.
Space rippled.
Energy signatures spiked.
A jump field formed.
Marcus stared at the sensor data.
“That’s a jump drive.”
Bella immediately nodded.
“It is.”
The readings were unlike anything they had ever seen before, but the underlying
principles appeared surprisingly familiar.
The object accelerated forward.
The distortion expanded.
And in the next instant it vanished.
Gone.
The jump signature lingered for several seconds before fading.
The bridge remained silent.
Finally Valencia spoke.
“Did that thing just use a jump drive?”
Bella was already reviewing the sensor logs.
“Something very close to one.”
James looked back out the window.
The realization was unsettling.
The massive alien vessel had employed a method of travel that appeared completely
beyond human understanding.
No charge sequence.
No visible field generation.
No detectable transition.
It had simply disappeared.
But the smaller object had used something else.
Something that looked almost familiar.
Almost understandable.
As if it had intentionally chosen to interact with humanity using technology closer to their
own level. Or perhaps it had been built specifically for that purpose. Neither possibility
made James feel any better.
Before anyone could speculate further, the communications console chimed.
An incoming transmission.
Admiral Bishop.
And somehow, that conversation suddenly seemed far more important than it had a
minute ago.


The station’s relay network established contact. A familiar face appeared on the bridge
displays.
Admiral Bishop.
The admiral smiled.
“Congratulations.”
Nobody responded.
Bishop continued.
“Successful arrival at Kemik Station. That’s one hell of a first jump.”
Still nothing.
The bridge camera automatically transmitted the crew’s video feed. Bishop finally saw
what was actually happening.
Six officers.
Standing around a table.
Drinking whiskey.
None of them at their stations.
None of them acting professionally.
None of them looking remotely happy.
The admiral’s expression immediately darkened.
“What in the hell am I looking at?”
Then he saw James.
The look on James’s face caused Bishop to stop mid-sentence.
The anger disappeared instantly.
In all the years he had known him, he had never seen James Bell look like that.
James looked exhausted.
Shaken.
Afraid.
Bishop immediately terminated the public channel. Seconds later a private
communication request appeared.
James accepted.
The bridge display shifted to Bishop’s office. Behind him stood several Colonial
Authority personnel and governor Princeton .
Every one of them looked confused.
Concerned.
Waiting for answers.
Bishop leaned forward.
“James.”
His voice was softer now.
“Is everyone okay?”
A pause.
“What happened?”
Nobody answered immediately.
Finally Jack spoke.
His Irish accent somehow even thicker than usual.
“You’re not gonna fucking believe this one, Bishop.”
The room fell silent.
Bishop stared at him.
Jack had never called him Bishop.
Not once.
It had always been Admiral.
Always.
The familiarity alone was enough to tell him something was very wrong.
James looked toward the display.
Then toward the bottle.
Then back at Bishop.
“We’re going to jump back.”
He picked up his glass.
“We’re going to drink.”
The crew nodded in agreement.
James took another sip.
Then looked directly into the camera.
“And you might want to start drinking now.”
A long pause.
“Because by the time I get back, you’re going to need it.”
For the first time since the call began, Bishop looked genuinely worried.
***

chapters.title: Witches at the Stake
chapters.text:
Excalibur jumped back to the shipyard approximately seven minutes and thirty-five
seconds after initially departing. The original jump had occurred at 12:05 PM. The
Colonial Authority had long ago standardized local timekeeping throughout Almagest
using the same fundamental system humanity had used back in Sol. It made scheduling,
navigation, logistics, and communication easier for every station, settlement, shipyard,
and ship operating in the system.
Excalibur reappeared at exactly 12:12:35 PM. Seven minutes and thirty-five seconds after
leaving.
It felt much longer.
The ship emerged just in front of the shipyard, facing the opposite direction from the one
it had been facing when it left.
For several moments, nobody on the bridge spoke. The crew remained gathered near the
small pedestal table, the bottle of Earth whiskey still open in front of them. None of them
were at their stations the way they should have been after a jump. None of them looked
ready to explain anything. James finally stepped toward the communications console.
“Bishop,” he said.
His voice was calm.
Too calm.
“Open a private channel.”
The ship’s computer automatically opened a secure private channel between James and
Bishop’s personal comms. James stepped back through the bridge hatch and into the
adjacent airlock compartment so the crew could not hear him.
Bishop appeared almost immediately.
Before the admiral could speak, James said, “Meet me at the Verdure Relay.”
Bishop frowned.
“The one you built?”
James nodded.
“The one with my cabin next to it.”
The relay station sat on the surface of Verdure. James had built it with extra materials left
over from earlier construction work. The Colonial Authority approved small personal
projects like that because participants in the colonization effort were expected to build
lives in Almagest, not merely work there. Small houses, farms, cabins, workshops, and
outposts had begun to appear across Verdure’s surface. Most were spread far enough
apart that they could barely be seen from the air, but they were there.
Humanity was starting to make the planet home.
James continued.
“Call everybody.”
Bishop’s expression shifted.
“Everybody?”
James stared at him.
“Everybody in the highest commands who is here needs to be there.”
Bishop understood immediately that this was not a routine incident.
James closed the communication window.
He stepped back onto the bridge.
The crew looked toward him.
Jack was still near the pilot’s station, waiting for orders.
James looked at him.
“Go to the plotted coordinates.”
Jack nodded.
“Aye, Captain.”
This would be Excalibur’s next test.
This time, however, the crew did not treat the ship with the same cautious uncertainty
they had used before. They had already tested her. Every system worked exactly how it
was supposed to.
The descent to Verdure began.
Artificial gravity held steady at one-quarter standard. The atmospheric lift thrusters
engaged automatically, exactly as designed. The ship descended toward the plotted point,
a small relay outpost beside James’s cabin.
The terrain below was open and quiet. From the air it looked mostly empty, but that was
deceiving. Verdure’s landscape was dotted with small homesteads, farms, and personal
structures built by people trying to create something normal in a system that had never
known humanity before. Excalibur dropped through the atmosphere smoothly. The
atmospheric thrusters adjusted without complaint.
Flight systems compensated for density changes.
Environmental systems stayed stable.
Power distribution remained clean.
The ship behaved perfectly.
After everything that had happened, that perfection almost felt strange. Excalibur
descended into an open field near the relay.
Her thrusters roared against the ground.
The landing gear extended with heavy mechanical certainty. Large struts lowered.
Hydraulic lines filled with fluid. Locking joints engaged. The massive square feet settled
into the snowdusted grass.
Then the engines powered down.
Silence returned.
Jack leaned back in the command chair and looked over his shoulder.
“She’s a pretty good fucking ride, sir.”
James knew Jack.
He knew exactly what that meant.
When Jack started getting formal, even a little bit, it meant he was scared out of his mind.
After that experience, James couldn’t blame him. James shut down the communications
array and looked at the crew.
They were all watching him.
Waiting.
Wondering what came next.
He had not told them.
James looked around the bridge and gave them a small smile.
“Well,” he said, “that little bit we had on the bridge was foreplay.”
A pause.
“Time to get the real party started.”
It was not a strong laugh that followed.
But it was a laugh.
At that moment, any laugh was worth having.
The crew disembarked shortly afterward.
A small deployable ladder extended from the side airlock. One by one, they climbed
down and jumped the last few feet onto Verdure.
Snow crunched under their boots.
For everyone except James, it was the first time they had laid their feet on the planet. In
the last hour, there had been moment after moment of life-changing, life-altering events
happening all at once.
The first successful flight of Excalibur.
The railgun tests.
The jump.
The alien ship.
The impossible power readings.
The capsule that had attached itself to the hull.
The impossible jump to Kemik.
The return.
Now, for a moment, the life-altering thing was peace.
The air was breathable.
The grass was real.
The snow was cold.
The world around them was barren in places, but alive. There were trees, leaves, plants,
and open fields that felt oddly familiar to Earth even though none of it was Earth.
It was peaceful.
And somehow that made everything worse and better at the same time. James and the
crew gathered at a park table outside the habitat cabin. A large bottle of alcohol sat on the
table.
The crew looked sad.
Shocked.
There was not one good word for it.
It was a mixture of overwhelming sadness, disbelief, concern, dread, and exhaustion.
Several shuttles began descending into the field. One after another, they landed near the
relay outpost.
The occupants disembarked slowly, looking around with the kind of concern people had
when they had been summoned somewhere without being told why.
More shuttles followed.
Then something larger descended from orbit. A modified Featherfall Freighter came
down in the opposite field, about forty-five degrees to the right of the main landing area.
It settled onto the terrain with surprising ease.
James raised his eyebrows and said out loud, “Well, I didn’t know this place was that flat,
we can land Excalibur and everyone from the station here.”
He nodded to himself.
“That worked out well.”
For a brief moment, James felt a small sense of pride.
He had picked a good spot.
It was a ridiculous thing to be proud of under the circumstances, but for that moment it
drowned out the rest of the feelings.
A group of the most important people in Almagest soon gathered near the weathered
picnic table.
Most of them looked annoyed.
A few looked impatient.
Some looked concerned.
All of them looked confused.
In the center of it all sat James Bell and his crew, drinking.
The contrast was almost comical.
The highest-ranking officials in the system had been summoned to an isolated relay
station on the surface of Verdure by a captain who refused to explain why. Naturally,
everyone assumed something had gone catastrophically wrong. The distant sound of
footsteps approached through the snow.
Bishop pushed his way through the crowd.
Unlike everyone else, he had apparently come prepared. He carried two bottles of
whiskey in each hand.
Four total.
The admiral with governor princeton in tow walked directly past several irritated officials
without acknowledging them.
James noticed immediately.
Today he was not smiling.
Not really.
The rest of the Almagest brass, or higher-ups, or whatever they liked to call themselves,
looked at Bishop with concern. To many of them, it must have seemed like some kind of
bad joke.
No one knew what was going on.
Only the crew knew what had happened.
There must have been more than ten of the highest-ranking officials on the Almagest
mission present.
Scientists.
Administrators.
Military officers.
Directors.
Governors.
Department heads.
People whose decisions affected every human being in Almagest.
James looked at Valencia and Bella.
“You guys snagged the information from the computer, right?”
Both nodded.
Valencia tapped a portable data drive resting on the table.
Bella held up a second backup copy.
James looked at Jack.
Jack nodded as well.
He knew what James needed him to get.
Sensor recordings.
Navigation logs.
Combat telemetry.
Visual recordings.
Everything.
Three independent copies.
No one was taking chances.
“All right, gentlemen,” James said. “Pile into my little home.”
James’s habitation module was simple.
A medium-sized rectangular structure built from leftover materials. Glass covered all
sides and much of the ceiling.
A large table sat in the middle.
There was a small kitchen module on one side and a bed on the other. The bed faced the
largest window in the habitat, positioned toward the sunrise and sunset.
It was not luxurious.
It was not impressive.
But it was his.
And until that day, it had been one of the quietest places in the entire system. James
motioned for the crew to bring the extra chairs stored in bins outside. He had figured he
would have company over at some point. Maybe friends from the shipyard.
Maybe a few people from the relay. Maybe Bishop if he ever decided to stop pretending
he was too important for simple things. Looking back, James never would have guessed
this would be the reason everyone came over.
The crew carried the chairs inside.
Everyone gathered around the table and sat down. The rest of the officials naturally
stayed on the opposite side of the table from where James stood. At the end of the table
sat one large leather chair James had brought in himself.
Everyone figured that was where he would sit.
One chair at the end of the table.
Facing everyone else.
The captain’s position.
But James ignored it.
The crew remained on the opposite side behind the gathered brass.
A quiet line formed in the room.
Leadership on one side.
Crew on the other.
James had already turned on the environmental systems to make sure the cabin was
warm, but not too warm.
Secondary systems were online too.
The ice maker in the freezer.
Extra refrigeration.
The small kitchen systems.
Whatever else might be needed.
James motioned for Bishop to come over
Bishop crossed the room and gave him the booze he brought while he stood near the
kitchen module, putting some of the bottles in the freezer and and one on the table with a
small pale of ice.
James leaned in and whispered.
“Daniel, I don’t know what the fuck just happened, but please believe me.”
Then James walked away.
For a moment Bishop did not move.
He simply watched him.
Bishop had known James for most of his life.
He knew when James was exaggerating.
He knew when James was joking.
He knew when James was lying.
This was none of those.
James was afraid.
The room settled.
James poured himself another drink.
Then he took a portable holo-table from storage and plugged in the data. He fumbled
around with an extension because there were three drives on the table, and the setup did
not immediately cooperate.
The first cable did not work.
The second adapter did not fit.
A scientist visibly sighed.
Several officials looked irritated.
James ignored them.
Eventually the holographic display activated.
The display showed the recording.
Not normal video.
The data consisted of telemetry and sensor interpretation. It did not begin with visuals. It
was everything the ship saw without any of the visual feed, converted by Excalibur’s
systems into what the ship understood had happened.
Sensor interpretation.
Navigation records.
Targeting data.
Power signatures.
Position tracking.
Timing logs.
The ship’s version of reality.
The video was paused initially.
James walked back over to the kitchen, opened a cabinet, pulled out a cigar, clipped it,
and lit it.
Several officials exchanged looks.
A few looked offended.
James did not care.
He looked back at the rest of the room with zero confidence.
“Let us know if you have any questions.”
Then the recording played.
The hologram showed the events as they happened.
The jump.
The violent emergence.
The tumble.
The systems failure.
The emergency reactor startup.
The alien vessel.
The power readings.
The weapons deployment.
The standoff.
The stand-down.
The disappearance.
The capsule.
The jump to Kemik.
Everything.
Nobody interrupted at first.
Nobody spoke.
The men and women were wide eyed.
The only sounds were the holo-table and the faint clink of glasses.
Then James noticed something odd again.
It was a distortion in the timeline.
One only James had picked up at first. He looked at Bella and Marcus quickly and then
back.
He was actually surprised Bella had not noticed it. When the ship got pulled out of jump
space, it appeared to happen only moments before they arrived at Kemik. But the
computer had recorded twelve extra minutes that apparently never happened.
Not in their heads.
Not a hallucination.
A computer reading.
From the most top-of-the-line sensors Almagest could provide.
James paused the video.
The image froze while Excalibur was still tumbling. He expanded the timeline and tapped
the holographic display.
“When we left the shipyard, it was 12:05 PM.”
Several people nodded.
“When we arrived at Kemik, it was 12:12 PM.”
Again, more nods.
Seven minutes and thirty-five seconds.
James pointed to the ship’s internal time.
Excalibur Internal Time: 12:24 PM.
The room became quiet.
Very quiet.
According to Excalibur, the ship was roughly twelve minutes older than the rest of the
galaxy. James pointed this out simply, tapping the holographic display.
Bella used her handheld device to push up the Solar System Standard Time recorded by
her watch. Her device had re-synced when she got back to the station. She had initially
assumed it was just a glitch.
The two times appeared side by side.
System Standard Time: 12:12 PM.
Excalibur Internal Time: 12:24 PM.
Exactly twelve minutes apart.
Not random.
Not drifting.
Not corrupted.
At first, James was wrong about what it meant. He suspected the time was missing from
the beginning of the event.
A lost section.
A gap.
Something that happened during the transition that nobody remembered. One of the
scientists in the room pointed it out.
“Captain Bell,” the scientist said carefully.
James looked at him.
The scientist expanded the timeline and several telemetry graphs.
“I don’t think time is missing from the beginning.”
James frowned.
“What are you saying?”
The scientist pointed at the data.
“The missing time is the time you were there. Not some random time you don’t
remember.”
James stared at him.
“You’re saying…”
The scientist looked uncomfortable.
“Mathematically, it’s impossible.”
A pause.
“But yes.”
Bishop, usually an extremely smart man whose patience had clearly run out, looked
across the room and raised his voice with all the command authority he possessed.
“Can someone please explain this shit to me?”
Several scientists jumped.
Prinston looked confused but also amused at Bishops outburst.
The room became silent.
The scientist took a breath.
“Whatever happened…”
He looked at the display.
“That ship either reversed time…”
He hesitated.
“Or made time not happen.”
He said it in a tone that made it sound like he was questioning himself.
James looked at Bishop.
“Basically, we got there.”
He pointed at the alien vessel.
“This shitshow happened.”
Then he pointed toward the capsule.
“And then that little device that hooked onto our ship—or something else—sent us back
in time and jumped us to the point we were supposed to be.”
The room went silent.
Governor Princeton was in the room too James noticed.
James suddenly realized he had completely ignored him and felt a little bad about it.
Princeton slowly raised his voice.
“I’ll take that drink now.”
For the first time all night, a small laugh moved through the room. James looked at him
and pointed, not aggressively, but in a my-man kind of way.
“Pour the man a drink .” gesturing towards Jack who had made his way with Valencia to
the kitchen.
Several people got up from the table and went to the kitchen to do the same thing.
The discussion lasted for hours.
The scientists all brought computers, as scientists do, and began going over the telemetry,
the video, every piece of data that came off Excalibur.
They reviewed the jump logs.
They reviewed the time logs.
They reviewed the sensor data.
They reviewed the navigation records.
They reviewed the power signatures.
They reviewed the capsule’s jump field.
They reviewed the alien ship’s energy readings.
They reviewed everything.
Some of them went directly to Excalibur and plugged into the ship’s computer to run
diagnostics multiple times.
Bella and Marcus accompanied them.
The rest of the higher-ups from the Colonial Authority, the ones who were not engineers
or scientists, sat around the table.
At first it was quiet.
Everyone sipped their drinks.
A few smoked.
They looked at each other with overwhelming shock and disbelief.
Eventually the discussion started again.
Questions were asked.
Then more questions.
Then arguments.
Then theories.
Hours and hours passed.
When everyone had arrived, it was around the middle of the day. High noon, or close to
it. Probably around one o’clock. The sun had been very high in the sky. By the time the
discussion began winding down, night had taken Verdure.
Luckily, Bishop’s modified Featherfall had a large set of crew quarters. James’s cabin
only had enough room for about four people. That night, everyone settled wherever they
could.
Some took bunks in Bishop’s ship.
Some unrolled sleeping bags on the floor of the cabin.
Some stayed inside the habitat.
Others stayed aboard the modified Featherfall.
Then they rested.
Or at least they tried to.
The next morning, James woke up with sunlight blasting directly into his face. He had
only actually experienced that a couple of times.
A real sunrise.
A real sky.
A real world under him.
His crew was there.
They were safe, at least for the moment.
One of his best friends, Daniel Bishop, was passed out in a habitat ten thousand years
away from home. James lay there for a moment and let the thought settle.
Then he got up.
He made a pot of coffee.
Then, realizing how many people were still scattered around his cabin and nearby, he
started a second. The smell began to make the people in his habitat stir.
Someone groaned.
Someone rolled over.
Someone else mumbled something that sounded vaguely threatening.
James poured himself a cup.
He liked it sweet.
Extra sugar.
Extra cream.
And a little bit of salt.
A habit he had no intention of explaining.
He went outside, walked to one of the external storage compartments, opened it, and
pulled out a folding beach chair.
He unfolded it.
Pointed it toward the sunrise.
And sat down.
For nearly thirty minutes, nobody needed anything from him.
It was quiet.
Peaceful.
After the last day, peace felt almost unnatural. Eventually Bishop and Jack walked over
together.
James glanced at them.
An unlikely bonding experience had apparently happened last night.
James pushed that thought aside.
At this point, he assumed they all needed to make as many friends as possible. He
gestured toward the cabin with his coffee mug.
“I made two pots. They’re there if you want any.”
Jack and Bishop both looked at each other and nodded.
Jack looked at James.
“That’ll happen here in a minute.”
His voice carried its usual witty, non-serious tone.
It was nice.
After everything that had happened, it was comforting.
Bishop grinned a little.
Then he became serious.
“There’s going to be a lot of meetings on this moving forward,” Bishop said. “Do you
even want to be part of it?”
James shook his head.
“No.”
James looked half way toward them He held up one finger.
“Number one. You cannot tell anybody about this.”
He held up a second.
“Number two. Take any and all of the data you want. Obviously, I don’t need to give you
permission to do that.”
He raised a third finger.
“Three…”
The words came out before he fully recognized what he was saying.
“I want to hunt this thing.”
The line landed hard.
James had not planned it.
It was just raw thought coming directly out of his mouth.
Bishop stared at him.
Jack stared at him.
Neither said anything at first.
James looked toward the sunrise.
The alien vessel.
The capsule.
The impossible power.
The missing twelve minutes.
All of it sat in his mind.
He was not done with it.
Not even close.
Humanity had crossed ten thousand years of darkness to reach Almagest.
Then the universe had answered back.
James took another sip of coffee.
“We found something yesterday.”
A pause.
“I want to know what it is.”
Jack smiled.
It was not a comforting smile.
It was the kind of smile that usually meant trouble.
“Well,” Jack said, brushing snow from his pants, “I was hoping you’d say that.”
Bishop closed his eyes and sighed.
Because he already knew.
Neither of them was going to let this go.
And if he was honest with himself, neither was he.

chapters.title: The Mundane
chapters.text:
Six months passed.
For James Bell, that was almost suspicious.
No alien ships.
No impossible jumps.
No mysterious capsules attaching themselves to Excalibur’s hull and dragging her across
space and time.
Just work.
Honest work.
The kind of work humanity had crossed ten thousand years to do.
Excalibur had become exactly what she had been designed to be.
A ship.
Not a prototype.
Not an experiment.
Not a miracle.
A ship.
She escorted cargo convoys through the outer belts. She carried Colonial Authority
officials between stations. She delivered habitation modules to distant moons and
outposts. She transported critical equipment wherever the growing colonies needed it.
And occasionally, she scared the hell out of pirates.
That part James enjoyed.
Some things, he had discovered, were universal.
No matter how far humanity traveled, no matter how advanced technology became, no
matter how many stars stood between civilization and Earth—
There would always be pirates.
Pirates loved desperation.
They loved isolation.
They loved people who couldn’t fight back.
The outer belts of Almagest provided all three.
Many of the ships operating beyond the populated regions looked like flying junkyards.
Captured freighters, salvaged mining ships, and broken colony-support vessels had been
welded together into bizarre creations that looked like they should have fallen apart years
ago.
Yet somehow they worked.
Sometimes alarmingly well.
The Colonial Authority didn’t possess enough ships to patrol everywhere.
Not yet.
Which meant Excalibur often found herself handling jobs that would normally belong to
a navy.
James didn’t mind.
Neither did the crew.
The routine was comforting.
After what they had seen, normality felt like a gift.
The idea for the sensor network began with a bottle of whiskey.
Most of James and Bishop’s plans did.
The two sat in Bishop’s office aboard Nostromo, staring at a tactical display that showed
the Almagest system.
The first capital ship in the system was nearly complete.
Even now, the vessel was enormous.
