Construction crews still moved across portions of the hull, but the majority of the ship
was operational.
Nostromo had been under construction since the earliest days of the colony effort.
After the incident with Excalibur, however, every priority in the system had quietly
shifted.
Nobody said it out loud.
Nobody needed to.
If there were things in Almagest that could casually generate that much power, humanity
wanted something bigger than a corvette.
Much bigger.
James sat back in his chair.
“It’s been an easy six months.”
Bishop looked up from a report.
“Easy?”
James shrugged.
“Relatively speaking.”
That earned a laugh.
“The crew’s getting settled on Excalibur. Things are good. The shipyard’s growing.
People are happy.”
He leaned back further.
“We even have a baby on the way.”
Bishop immediately smiled.
“I saw that.”
He nodded.
“I’ll send my congratulations personally.”
A pause.
“That’s the first new baby we’ve had in the system.”
Another pause.
“At least the first one we know about.”
James laughed.
“Probably.”
The office door slid open.
Governor Princeton stepped inside carrying a stack of paperwork that immediately made
both men feel sorry for him.
Princeton was one of those rare people who genuinely enjoyed helping others.
James found that quality vaguely suspicious.
The governor smiled as he entered.
“Am I interrupting?”
“Only paperwork,” Bishop said.
“Then you’re welcome.”
James grinned.
“Hey, Princeton.”
The governor looked over.
“I heard you finally got your flag planted on Verdure.”
Princeton nodded.
James pointed at him.
“So when are we going fishing?”
The governor blinked.
“Fishing?”
“Yeah.”
“There aren’t any fish.”
James frowned.
“That sounds like a problem.”
“The planet is barren.”
Bishop suddenly looked up.
“Not for much longer.”
Both men turned toward him.
The admiral tapped a report.
“We got confirmation this morning.”
James immediately sat forward.
“The breeding ship?”
Bishop nodded.
“The one carrying the genetic archives and animal propagation facilities.”
A smile spread across Princeton’s face.
“When?”
“Three months.”
For a moment nobody spoke.
Then all three men smiled.
Humanity had survived.
Humanity had built stations.
Humanity had built ships.
But life?
Real life?
That was different.
This was the next step.
Livestock.
Wildlife.
Ecosystems.
The beginning of a living world.
Princeton slowly sat down.
“We need to start reserve protocols.”
Bishop nodded.
“I already have teams preparing surveys.”
James nodded too.
This mattered.
Humanity had made mistakes on Earth.
Huge mistakes.
The people of Almagest had an opportunity to do better.
This time they had the knowledge.
This time they had the technology.
This time they had the luxury of planning ahead.
Protected reserves would be established before development reached those regions.
Some places would remain untouched from the very beginning.
For once, humanity might get it right.

Governor Princeton looked across the desk.

The door opened.

Another man entered behind the scientist who had initially corrected James about the
missing time.

James watched him quietly as the man took a seat and began organizing his paperwork.

He's the kind of person we should take if we ever find this thing, James thought.

Bishop stood and swiped the holographic display mounted on the wall behind him.

A three-dimensional map of the Almagest system appeared.

Thousands of small icons illuminated the display.

“Our sensor relay network,” Bishop said.

He zoomed the display outward.

“These are all of the relay satellites we've been able to deploy.”

A brief pause.

He highlighted a cluster of signatures deep within the Byblos sector.

“We're getting power readings consistent with a colony ship in this sector.”

The room immediately became quiet.
“We've sent several long-range drones,” Bishop continued, “but none of them have
managed to get close enough to capture any useful data.”

He looked around the room.

“This...”

He hesitated.

“This is highly concerning.”

Another swipe brought up the recorded power signatures.

“We do not need a war during the first five years we're in a new system.”

Governor Princeton looked toward the display.

James did the same.

The scientist beside him slowly leaned forward.

None of them liked what they were seeing.

James looked deeply at the display, analyzing every detail.

Admiral Bishop watched him for a moment.

“We don't have much yet,” Bishop said, “but I sense that you're paying attention to
something more than the rest of us.”

James kept his eyes on the holographic map.

Then he looked over at the scientist.

“Go ahead.”

The scientist looked up.

James nodded toward Bishop.

“Tell him what you told me earlier today.”

The scientist shifted slightly in his chair.

He was nervous.
Not because he had said anything wrong.

Because the information itself was concerning.

“The location Excalibur jumped to,” the scientist said.

He paused for a long moment.

“Was roughly in that region.”

The room went cold.

Bishop said nothing.

He didn't need to.

He had an analytical mind, and he understood exactly what that meant.

Whatever was happening in that sector was happening near Byblos.

Maybe not on the planet itself.

Maybe not on its moon.

Maybe simply somewhere in the surrounding region.

They did not know yet.

James stared at the cluster of signatures on the display.

For a moment, the room around him seemed to fade.

There could be an entire civilization we haven't even been able to see in that sector,
James thought.

Waiting for us.

Governor Princeton seemed calculating in that moment, thinking through the entirety of
what had just been explained to him.

He was not a scientist.

He was not a military man.

He was simply a civilian, someone entrusted with making decisions that would affect the
entire Verdeur colony.
He looked across the room at the three men.

“Six months ago, as you know, I authorized this research project and classified all of the
information we're discussing.”

His expression hardened.

“So, no discussing any of this outside this room, as you've already been told.”

He looked at each of them individually.

“Anything moving forward is to be discussed between the four of us and anybody I
personally read in.”

He paused.

“There are a few higher-level officials who have already been read in. Mostly politicians,
really. No one too important.”

A small smile crossed his face.

“And the rest of the people who were there the day that the thing…”

He looked over at James and gave a small snicker.

“…stole you.”

The room chuckled quietly.

“So,” Princeton continued, “we have quite a bit to go over and a lot of work to do.”

“Thankfully, the last couple of months have been relatively smooth sailing.”

“The project has been in full swing.”

“Excalibur seems to be performing well.”

“Nostromo is nearing completion.”

“The shipyard, along with the adjacent stations we've been building, has been operating
smoothly.”

“The colonization effort is generally going according to plan…”

He paused.
“…except for the obvious missing colony ships.”

The room grew quiet again.

“The good news,” he continued, “is that we have the breeding ship on the way.”

“Hopefully, within the next couple of months, we can finally start proper farms.”

A grin appeared.

“And maybe get some proper beef on everybody's plates instead of the frozen shit we've
been eating for a while.”

Admiral Bishop laughed.

He stood, walked over to a small cabinet built into the wall, opened it, and pulled out a
bottle along with several glasses.

Without asking, he poured everyone in the room a drink.

“Well…”

He raised his glass.

“Cheers to that, gentlemen.”

The scientist politely declined.

James certainly did not.

Neither did Governor Princeton.

The three men raised their glasses together before taking a drink.

Bishop set his glass down and looked around the room.

“Is there anything else, gentlemen?”

Governor Princeton shook his head.

“Just a few things between me and you.”

He nodded toward Bishop.

“But otherwise…”
“…nothing of great importance.”

Bishop looked over toward James and the scientist.

“You're dismissed, gentlemen.”

A small smile crossed his face.

“Have a good one.”

“Stay safe.”

“And fly high.”

chapters.title: Untitled
chapters.text:
The colony ship arrived exactly ninety-two days later.
The celebrations started before it even entered orbit.
Stations launched fireworks.
Workers received time off.
Parties broke out across nearly every inhabited facility in the system.
For the first time since arriving in Almagest, people felt like they were building a future
instead of merely surviving.
James watched the arrival from Excalibur’s bridge.
The colony ship drifted through space like a small city.
Thousands of people lined observation decks across multiple stations to watch.
It felt important.
Because it was.
Without animal life, agriculture remained difficult.
Food production existed, but entire ecological chains were missing.
Now livestock would arrive.
Birds.
Pollinators.
Working animals.
The foundations of complete ecosystems.
The future had just entered orbit.
James smiled.
Then frowned.
Jack noticed immediately.
“What’s wrong?”
James stared out the window.
“My dog.”
Jack blinked.
“Your what?”
“My dog.”
Valencia laughed.
“You still thinking about that?”
“Of course I am.”
The dog had been scheduled to arrive aboard another colony ship.
One carrying a limited allotment of preserved companion animals.
Only one hundred twenty-two pets had been approved.
James had somehow managed to secure a slot.
Jack looked at him.
“You’ve been thinking about a dog for ten thousand years?”
“Yes.”
“That’s insane.”
“I know.”
Valencia shook her head.
“I’d forgotten about that.”
James sighed.
Unfortunately, animal cryogenic survival rates were considerably worse than human
rates.
The reports weren’t encouraging.
Bella quietly looked over from her console.
“Maybe you’ll get lucky.”
James nodded.
Maybe.
He hoped so.

chapters.title: Untitled
chapters.text:
Later that afternoon, James, Bishop, and Princeton stood together on Nostromo’s
observation deck.
Below them, Excalibur floated just off the capital ship’s port side.
The corvette looked small compared to Nostromo.
Yet James’s eyes always found her first.
Home.
That was the only word he could think of anymore.
Home.
Not Earth.
Not Sol.
Not the places he remembered.
Excalibur.
Verdure.
The crew.
The settlement.
That was home now.
Bishop suddenly frowned.
He had remembered something.
“Oh.”
James looked over.
“What?”
The admiral folded his arms.
“One of the sensor relays picked up something strange.”
That immediately got both men’s attention.
“What kind of strange?” Princeton asked.
Bishop looked directly at James.
“The power signature matches the readings we recorded during the incident.”
Silence.
For a moment nobody moved.
Princeton looked worried.
James smiled.
Bishop immediately recognized the smile.
“Our plan is working,” James said.
Bishop nodded.
The sensor network already contained over five hundred relay satellites spread
throughout the system.
Five hundred and twenty-two, to be exact.
Not enough.
But enough to start finding things.
Princeton looked back and forth between them.
“You realize the only thing that went right during that encounter was you powering down
your weapons.”
James laughed.
“Probably.”
“No, definitely.”
Bishop laughed too.
Princeton pointed at him.
“At least you apparently have some diplomatic skills.”
James raised an eyebrow.
“I’ll take that as a compliment.”
“You should.”
Princeton smiled.
“I didn’t expect diplomacy from the captain of a ship carrying a railgun that size.”
All three men laughed.
It felt good.
There was rank.
There was authority.
There was a chain of command.
But underneath it all, they were building a civilization together.
Everybody knew each other.
Everybody worked together.
Everybody trusted each other.
It felt less like a government and more like a family.
At least for now.

chapters.title: Untitled
chapters.text:
The crew spent much of those six months building something else.
Homes.
Actual homes.
Small cabins appeared near James’s relay station one after another.
Bella and Valencia built theirs together.
Marcus and Jack built theirs together.
Nobody really planned it.
The settlement simply happened.
One structure at a time.
One project at a time.
One weekend at a time.
Every morning they gathered around the same old picnic table James had owned for
years.
Coffee.
Breakfast.
Conversation.
The table was beginning to show its age.
The wood had weathered.
Several boards needed replacement.
Nobody cared.
The Colonial Authority eventually approved construction of a small fuel-processing
station nearby.
Now Excalibur could land directly beside the settlement.
The massive corvette towered above the cabins whenever she touched down.
A fortress watching over a village.
It was strangely comforting.
The ship felt like home.
The settlement felt like home.
Verdure felt like home.
Almagest felt like home.
And every member of the crew knew it.


Life on the frontier remained difficult.
Crops failed.
Equipment broke.
Ships exploded.
Usually by accident.
Sometimes not.
Entire colony ships occasionally disappeared.
That part bothered James.
The Third Colony Ship never arrived.
The Fifth Colony Ship never arrived.
No distress calls.
No debris.
No survivors.
Nothing.
James found himself thinking about it more often than he liked.
The dog bothered him.
Five thousand missing people bothered him much more.
Entire colony ships did not simply vanish.
Not anymore.
Every vessel was tracked.
Every vessel communicated.
Every vessel remained connected to the growing network humanity had spent years
building.
There should have been no way for that to happen.
No way at all.
James stood outside his cabin one evening watching the sunset over Verdure.
The lights of Excalibur glowed softly in the distance.
Behind him, he could hear laughter coming from the other cabins.
His crew.
His family.
Safe.
For now.
The breeze moved through the grass.
The world felt peaceful.
Normal.
Almost perfect.
James smiled.
Everyone thought the hard days were over.
Anyone who knew better understood that wasn’t true.
But things were good.
So everyone enjoyed them while they could.

Life in Almagest got better after the breeding colony ship arrived.

Real farms began to appear across Verde.

Livestock multiplied.

Fields expanded.
Large free-range ranches stretched across valleys that had been untouched only months
before.

It was honest work.

Elegant in its simplicity.

A path humanity had never truly taken before.

This time they had the opportunity to build things correctly.

The nature preserves established during the first years of colonization quickly filled with
life.

Thousands of animals roamed freely.

Entire ecosystems were carefully reconstructed from the genetic libraries brought from
Earth.

Predators.

Prey.

Birds.

Insects.

Everything was introduced slowly and methodically, allowing nature to establish itself
without repeating the ecological mistakes humanity had made back home.

Within three months, nearly ten thousand animals representing almost every major
species had been released across Verde.

For the first time in ten thousand years, humanity was not simply surviving on an alien
world.

It was watching one come alive.

Even James's cabin, perched high above the surrounding valleys with the rest of his
crew's small settlement, wasn't far enough away to escape it.

Every now and then a bird would land on the roof of his hab, singing to itself as the sun
rose over the mountains.
Occasionally a squirrel would decide that one of the nearby trees made an excellent place
to bury food.

Sometimes James would simply sit outside with a cup of coffee before work, listening.

Birdsong.

Wind through the trees.

Leaves rustling.

It almost sounded like Earth.

Almost.

For a few quiet moments each morning, it was easy to forget they were ten thousand
years from home.

There was even a small farm at the bottom of the valley that one of the engineers had
started.

James had introduced him to the area where he and his crew had built their homes, but
very deliberately made one thing clear.

“You're not allowed to settle right next to me.”

The engineer had looked confused.

James simply shrugged.

“I don't like having neighbors.”

A pause.

“And I sure as hell don't want an HOA starting.”

The engineer laughed.

He took James's advice and built his farm a comfortable distance down the valley.

Far enough away that they each had their own space.

Close enough that if either one needed help, the other wasn't far away.

Over the years the two became good friends, despite seeing each other only occasionally.
Life in Almagest had a way of keeping everyone busy.

Whenever Excalibur returned from one of her long patrols or transport missions, the
engineer somehow always seemed to know.

James and the crew would usually find a crate sitting outside one of the habs.

Fresh vegetables.

Fruit.

Milk.

Eggs.

Occasionally a few cuts of fresh beef after animals started getting distributed in bulk.

Things that had become almost luxurious after years of frozen rations and processed
food.

The engineer never asked for anything in return.

He always said the same thing.

"You guys are the reason any of this exists."

James never really knew how to respond to that.

So he usually settled for helping fix a tractor, replacing a broken pump, or spending an
afternoon mending a fence before heading back into space.

It was a fair trade.

And in its own quiet way, it reminded all of them that they weren't just building ships
anymore.

They were building a home not just a home they were building life not A LIFE but LIFE
on a distant world.

chapters.title: Another Day
chapters.text:
Almagest Standard Date: Year 3, Day 182​
Approximately three and a half years after humanity’s arrival in the Almagest.
The day was going well.

James sat leisurely in the command chair.

Valencia sat to his left.

Marcus sat to his right.

Bella, per usual, was holding the handrailing behind Marcus and using her portable pad to
do whatever work she needed to.

Bella glanced over at Marcus's console.

“Is that...?”

Marcus studied the display for another second.

He looked back at her.

“I don't think so.”

Jack sat at a console newly installed just to the rear of the bridge, planning routes for the
job that they were on.

Jack was loving life.

After the maiden voyage of Excalibur, James had personally requested that a permanent
flight station be installed on the bridge specifically for him.

From that point forward, James almost exclusively let Jack fly Excalibur.

The captain's chair technically belonged to James.

In practice, everyone aboard knew it belonged to Jack.

All five of them joked, laughed, and had a good time while still working, doing a job that
needed to get done.

Bella and James had always been close.

They were the older members of the crew.

James had met Bella at a bar during one of his freight routes through the outer belt.
He hadn't been there more than a few minutes before he noticed a commotion across the
room.

Two men, both much bigger than Bella, had decided bothering her was somehow a good
idea.

James watched for a moment.

Bella didn't need help.

She was already in the middle of telling both of them exactly what she thought of them,
loud enough that the entire bar could hear.

The two men eventually backed down, deciding she wasn't worth the trouble.

James couldn't help but laugh.

A man sitting beside him at the bar noticed.

“You know her?” he asked.

James shook his head.

The man snorted.

“She works on my ship.”

There was a long pause before he took another drink.

“She is an absolute handful.”

Another pause.

“You want her?”

James looked over toward Bella.

She was still glaring at the two men as they hurried toward the exit.

He smiled.

“Sure.”

The other captain didn't even hesitate.

“Good.”
“You can keep her.”

James never looked back.

Neither did Bella.

She walked straight over to James, who by this point was simply standing there beside
her former captain, watching the whole thing unfold.

Stopping directly in front of him, she looked him up and down.

“You want what they got?” she asked aggressively.

James looked over at the other captain.

Then back at Bella.

A grin slowly spread across his face.

“I think I like her.”

Bella turned toward her former captain.

“Fuck off.”

She jabbed a finger toward the ship outside.

“I don't want to be on that shithole anymore anyway.”

She took a step toward the door before looking back one last time.

“I'm done.”

“You fucking rat.”

James almost fell in love.

Not romantically.

He simply loved people who could stand up for themselves.

Especially against people bigger than they were.

Especially when it cost them something.

As Bella started walking away, James reached out and gently grabbed her forearm.
“Hold on.”

She turned, looking ready for another fight.

“So...”

James shrugged.

“You need a job now or what?”

Bella raised an eyebrow.

James nodded toward the docking bays.

“We're looking for an engineer.”

“The guy I've got is still pretty new.”

Bella looked at him for a long moment.

Then back toward the bar.

Then toward the ship she'd just quit.

A small grin finally appeared.

“When do we leave?”

Marcus,Valencia, and Jack were all in their early twenties—just enough experience to do
the job, but not long enough to have the wisdom to stay alive while doing it.

Even during that first encounter, Bella had shown what she was capable of.

She had saved the ship and the crew from tumbling and it wasn't the first time.

That could have been really bad in zero gravity.

James looked out across the bridge.

Three cargo ships drifted ahead of Excalibur, the corvette escorting them through open
space.

It was just another day.

Pings here and there, but nothing too crazy.
Excalibur didn’t initially have long-range comms and relied on the stations for long-range
communications.

Recently, though, there had been an upgrade to the front of the ship, allowing for a large
detector and a large antenna relay, giving Excalibur long-range communication
capability.

The modifications also added a small processing and drilling facility that allowed
components to be manufactured and repaired while underway.

Marcus had installed all of the upgrades himself.

Marcus looked over at James.

“Transmission incoming.”

He glanced down at his console.

“It’s from Governor Princeton.”

James waved his communication device, and Governor Princeton appeared on the
holographic display in front of him.

“Hello, ladies and gentlemen,” Princeton said.

“We have some news. When you’re done with the current mission you’re on, meet us
back at the shipyard.”

He paused for a moment.

“It should be in about… what… three days? You’ll be back?”

James looked up at the governor.

“Sounds about right. Everything’s looking pretty clean out here.”

Bella immediately reached forward and smacked James on the back of the head.

“You’re not supposed to say things like that.”

She folded her arms.

“You know that’s bad luck.”

A loud snicker came from the back of the bridge.
Jack.

James slowly turned toward Bella with an annoyed look before raising his voice.

“Computer.”

“Save date.”

“Set route.”

“And set timer.”

The ship’s computer replied in its usual robotic tone.

“Confirmed.”

Princeton nodded.

“See you soon.”

The communication ended.

Based on what James and Admiral Bishop had been discussing over the previous several
weeks, James already had a general idea of what the meeting might be about.

The satellite network had now grown to over two thousand sensor satellites spread
throughout the system, most concentrated around Verdure.

The colonization effort still centered around the single planet.

Most colony ships continued arriving there.

Shipyards.

Habitats.

Small farms.

Fuel stations.

Manufacturing centers.

Everything continued to expand around Verdure.

Excalibur, however, had quietly been expanding the network every time she left port.
While transporting materials from sparse mining operations around Kemik and
throughout the Biblos Sector, the crew would periodically deploy another group of sensor
satellites.

Excalibur could carry roughly twenty-four satellites in her hangar at one time.

Every mission became another opportunity.

Every gap in coverage slowly disappeared.

James simply plotted where the holes were.

The crew would pass through.

Another satellite would quietly drift into position.

Over time, the network spread farther and farther into the outer system.

There had been a few unusual pings.

Mostly throughout the Bilo Sector and portions of the outer asteroid fields.

Nothing particularly concerning.

Whatever they were detecting seemed to keep its distance.

If that was what it was doing.

James and Admiral Bishop routinely reviewed every report together.

Captain Ferguson joined them regularly.

Governor Princeton attended whenever he was available.

Along with several engineers and scientists who had been read into the incident from the
very beginning.

Most of the other Colonial Authority officials who had been present at James’s cabin that
first day had chosen not to remain involved.

It was a decision James understood.

Valencia looked back at Jack.

Jack wore the same concerned expression.
He spoke up.

“Captain…”

He let it hang for a second.

Again.

James didn’t like this unusual formality.

He knew something stupid—or concerning—was about to be said.

Whether it was stupid, concerning, or both, James didn’t know quite yet.

Without fully turning around, James looked halfway over his shoulder, silently letting
Jack know he was listening.

Jack met his eyes.

“Is that about… the thing?”

He hesitated.

“Did we finally catch something in our little net that we’ve been making?”

Bella looked over at Jack with an impressed expression.

She and James were the only members of the crew who had been actively involved in that
effort. Jack, although eager, hadn’t been directly involved with the program.

Bella raised an eyebrow.

“Well, aren’t we being observant today?”

Jack looked back at her with his typical Irish accent.

“Do you think I can’t learn?”

He let it hang there for a few seconds before adding,

“Ma’am.”

The bridge fell quiet for half a second.

The running joke about Bella being older than the rest of the crew had been going back
and forth for months now.
James had to admit—

It was still funny.

Bella immediately looked like she wanted to get violent.

James let out a hearty chuckle.

Marcus joined him.

James looked around at everyone.

“Yep.”

He nodded toward Jack.

“Jack’s right.”

“I want all of you there.”

“This one… we think we got something big.”

He shrugged.

“It might be nothing.”

“But it also could be big.”

“So… I guess we’ll see in a few days.”

Right on cue, Jack nodded.

“Aye, Captain.”

He looked back down at his console.

While everyone else’s attention was still on James, Jack quietly added,

“Three hours until we arrive.”

Bella glanced at the navigation display.

“Sounds about right.”

James turned back toward his own console.
Already knowing the answer, he raised his voice to no one in particular.

“Do we have anything?”

“Long-range scan?”

“Short-range scan?”

“Anything?”

chapters.title: FIRE AND BLOOD..AND A NEW GHOST
chapters.text:
At that point, the irony was palpable.

A contact suddenly appeared on the tactical display.

One hundred and twenty kilometers away.

Closing.

They were burning straight toward them.

Bella instinctively started to reach over to slap James in the back of the head again.

She stopped herself.

“I’ll be down in the CIC.”

She pointed toward Marcus.

“Prepare engineering for a potential combat scenario.”

she turned and headed toward the rear airlock down the stairs through the airlock to
commons and towards the right side of the room where the entry to the CIC was located.

Excalibur had been running cold and in the middle of the formation of cargo ships to
mask their signature

James looked over at Marcus.

“Warm us up.”
He nodded toward the contact.

“I want them to know we’re here.”

Immediately, Excalibur roared to life.

Every reactor came online.

The ship had been quietly coasting alongside the cargo convoy for hours.

Not anymore.

She was awake.

Ready for battle.

The XR-9 railgun began charging.

Reactors surged online.

Thrusters roared to life throughout the ship.

The bridge lights flickered once before dimming into the deep red combat lighting.

Over the intercom, Bella’s voice echoed throughout the ship.

“All hands, buckle up.”

“Let’s hit it.”

James looked around the bridge and yelled,

“Buckle up!”

One by one, the crew secured themselves into their seats.

Helmet seals locked.

Communications were checked.

Each member went down the checklist.

“James, green light.”

“Valencia, green light.”
“Marcus, green light.”

“Jack, green light.”

A second later Bella’s voice came back over the intercom.

“Bella, green light.”

James looked toward Jack.

Since the pilot sat slightly higher than everyone else, James simply held up a thumbs-up.

“Punch it.”

The rear thruster array ignited.

Excalibur leapt forward.

The ship was capable of accelerating at nearly thirty five Gs under maximum forward
thrust.

For any extended period of time, that kind of acceleration was certain death.

Typical combat scenarios rarely exceeded nine Gs.

Nine was uncomfortable.

Fifteen was punishment.

Jack ignored what was comfortable.

He pushed Excalibur into a reckless twelve-G burn.

The corvette lunged toward the five unidentified contacts, one with a signature that
Marcus was trying to resolve.

Marcus’s voice came over the helmet communications.

“Depressurizing.”

Warning lights flashed as atmospheric pressure vented from sections of the ship in
preparation for combat.

The contacts were now seventy-five kilometers away.

Almost within railgun range.
James keyed the open communications onto all frequencies.

“This is the warship Excalibur.”

His voice deepened.

“Fuck off…”

He smiled.

“…and I won’t make a game out of ripping your pieces-of-shit ships apart.”

James loved this part.

He always deepened his voice when he made threats like that.

Valencia spoke over the internal communications.

“Point-defense cannons online.”

“Belts good.”

“Railgun ready to go.”

She glanced at the tactical display.

“Fifty kilometers and closing.”

“Maximum effective range is forty-five.”

She looked over at James.

“Let me know if you want me to hit them.”

Marcus studied the sensor returns.

“Doesn’t look like they’re shying away from a fight.”

Valencia raised her voice.

“Closing speed, two thousand meters per second.”

James looked toward Jack.

“Give us a decel burn.”
“Flip and burn.”

“Give me about eight hundred meters per second of closing rate.”

He looked toward Valencia.

“Warm up the railgun.”

“As soon as they hit forty kilometers…”

He smiled.

“Fuck them up.”

Valencia and Jack screamed a loud war cry over the comms

Valencia did exactly what James asked.

The moment the contacts crossed thirty-five kilometers, the XR-9 Godspear roared.

It sounded like a dragon burning a village.

The entire ship lurched as the railgun discharged, the ship flowing into the plasma from
the railgun. It was beautiful like a wave of every color washing over the front of the ship.

The rear thruster array immediately compensated for the recoil, holding Excalibur steady.

Only two seconds later, Valencia spoke.

“Splash one.”

James couldn’t help but grin.

At that particular moment, he realized something.

The biggest strength of Excalibur wasn’t the fact that she carried a big-ass railgun.

It was the fact that she could fire it every four seconds.

“Charging.”

The familiar hum filled the ship again.

Four seconds later—

The railgun fired.
“Splash two.”

Another four seconds.

The XR-9 roared again.

“Splash three.”

Four more seconds.

Another thunderous discharge.

“Splash four.”

Four of the five ships were gone.

They hadn’t even managed to return fire.

It was a bloodbath.


Marcus screamed.

“Incoming!”

Real panic.

Jack reacted before anyone else even had time to think.

In half a second, he rotated Excalibur ninety degrees.

The main thrusters fired for another half second.

Then he rolled the ship back toward the target they had been closing on.

The maneuver peaked at nearly thirteen Gs.

Marcus blacked out almost instantly.

Only for a second or two.

James was right on the edge himself.

Valencia and Jack didn’t even budge.
Another railgun shot screamed toward the target.

Then another.

Another.

Then another.

Four railgun rounds hit the target.

The ship shouldn’t have had a power signature anymore.

Valencia looked over at Marcus.

Seeing him slumped over his console, she immediately pulled the sensor suite onto the
holographic display to her left.

She screamed.

“Incoming!”

“Incoming!”

“Incoming!”

James immediately recognized what it had to be.

Heavy cannon fire.

Not quite a railgun.

But pretty damn close.

The first round slammed into one of the forward armor plates.

It ricocheted away into space.

Three more impacts followed almost immediately.

One skipped across the top of the bridge.

Barely.

Another struck the bow head-on, disabling one of Excalibur’s retro thrusters before
punching all the way through the hangar bay and finally stopping against the forward face
of the reactor citadel.
Marcus suddenly came back around.

“Five kilometers!”

That was all James needed.

He took the conn.

Overriding Jack’s pilot controls and Valencia’s weapon controls, James threw the ship
into a violent maneuver.

Excalibur yawed horizontally while pitching and while entering a slight angled spin.

At the same time, James pushed the ship into another twelve-G burn, slowly rotating the
hull as they accelerated.

It was an incredibly dangerous maneuver.

A cannon screamed past the ship.

Close.

So close it shouldn’t have missed.

James keyed the intercom.

“We’re fighting someone who knows what they’re doing!”

“This shit we’re fighting is much larger than the signature says it is!”

“Give me a visual!”

Within half a second, the tactical display switched to live imaging.

James stared at the screen.

It wasn’t a pirate corvette.

It wasn’t a frigate.

It looked closer to a battlecruiser.

Very obviously of Earth design.

Or at least human.
There was still patchwork visible across portions of the hull, but far less than the typical
pirate craft.

Two massive cannon assemblies sat along the dorsal and ventral hull.

At the bow protruded what looked like a small railgun.

James processed the information almost instantly.

The railgun hadn’t fired once during the engagement.

That meant one thing.

It probably wasn’t operational.

Everyone was beginning to black out.

James and Valencia were barely hanging on.

The maneuver James was flying was the only reason they were still alive.

Several more cannon rounds slammed into Excalibur.

One hitting the rear hydrogen tank housing and another skipping off of the hull just in
front of the bridge

Smaller impacts this time.

But they shattered the first two layers of armored bridge glass.

At that point they were practically point-blank.

Both ships’ point-defense cannons were lighting each other up.

James stopped the acceleration burn.

He rotated the ship horizontally.

Valencia did her job.

Damn well.

She placed the XR-9 directly on the enemy reactor.

Then she pulled the trigger.
She basically executed the poor cruiser.

The ship exploded.

A part of the ship slammed into the upper deck of excalibur but was mostly stopped by
the superstructure

James turned toward Valencia to say something.

She wasn’t talking.

Before he could ask why—

Marcus screamed.

“Valencia!”

Then he passed out.

James looked over.

Marcus had been hit.

A large piece of shrapnel had buried itself deep into his chest.

James’s eyes immediately shifted toward Valencia.

It looked like something had taken a bite out of her arm.

Blood poured across her console.

Only then did James finally look down at himself.

A large piece of shrapnel was sticking out of his leg.

He hadn’t even felt it.

Not yet.

Adrenaline was one hell of a drug.

Jack sat behind the second layer of armored bridge glass.

At that particular moment, he was the luckiest person on the bridge.

The bridge windows had failed after the explosion.
Nobody had noticed.

There had simply been too much happening.

Everyone had been half blacked out.

The entire bridge was nearly blown open, everyone's suits were venting the atmosphere
from shrapnel.

Something large had struck the top of it.

Something explosive.

Maybe a torpedo.

Maybe a missile.

Maybe just another cannon round.

James didn’t know.

He stabilized the ship with a short corrective burn, placing Excalibur onto an intercept
course with the cargo ships they had been escorting.

He switched on the autopilot.

Then immediately began unstrapping himself.

Jack, completely uninjured, made the correct call.

Honestly…

A pretty impressive one.

He keyed the intercom.

“Bella!”

“Don’t come up to the bridge!”

“Contacts dealt with, multiple casualties repressurise commons”

Bella answered instantly.

“Copy!”
Jack was already yelling again.

“Get the medical shit out !”

“We’re coming down!”

“We have three casualties! We got one hard down”

That didn’t sit right with Bella.

Jack moved with a swiftness James had never seen before.

Jack had always been good at his job.

Occasionally even great.

But this…

This was adrenaline.

Training.

Pure instinct taking over.

In what felt like one second, Jack had all three of them unstrapped.

James.

Valencia.

Marcus.

Then he somehow dragged nearly five to six hundred pounds of wounded crew—not
including their suits—into the airlock where Bella was already waiting.

James looked over at them.

“Deal with Marcus and Valencia.”

“I’ll tourniquet myself.”

He did it with a speed that suggested experience.

He had it.

The scars proved it.
James looked down at the piece of metal sticking out of his leg.

It wasn’t buried very deep.

It didn’t appear to have hit a major artery.

He grabbed it.

Pulled it free.

And tossed it onto the deck.

Marcus was carried into Main Commons.

Valencia, despite having an entire chunk of her arm missing, was still on her feet.

She was helping carry Marcus.

With that arm.

Bella pulled a tourniquet from the medical bag without hesitation.

She wrapped it around Valencia’s upper arm, about three inches below her shoulder.

Then she cinched it down.

James didn’t remember much of what happened next.

He remembered flashes.

Bella shouting orders.

Jack dragging people through the ship.

Marcus screaming after he woke back up.

Valencia refusing to stop helping even with half her arm torn apart.

Medical equipment scattered across Main Commons.

Blood on the deck.

The rest came in pieces.

Shock had a way of stealing memories.
James had been through more fights than he cared to count.

Boarding actions.

Pirate ambushes.

Fleet engagements.

Running battles through asteroid fields.

He had nearly died more than once.

But never…

Never had he fought something with such a massive difference in capability between two
ships.

Months later, sitting aboard the shipyard and looking out across the stars, James found
himself thinking back to that fight.

Excalibur had won.

On paper.

The pirate cruiser had been destroyed, or at least what we thought was a pirate.

The cargo convoy had survived.

The mission had been successful.

But James didn’t feel victorious.

He looked out toward the endless darkness beyond the station.

He had an incredible crew.

Every one of them.

Jack’s flying had kept them alive.

Valencia had put every railgun round exactly where it needed to go.

Bella had saved the ship, and Marcus.

Again.
Marcus had continued doing his job right up until the moment he was hit and to James
that was a real show of how far he had come from when he had found him..

They were professionals.

The best crew a captain could ever ask for.

They should never have survived that encounter.

And honestly…

They barely did.

chapters.title: RECOVERY AND RECONSTUCTION
chapters.text:
Jack got the ship back in an instant.

He pulled an emergency jump directly back to the shipyard, where the extensive medical
facilities were waiting.

Bella was still tending to the wounds James, Valencia, and Marcus had suffered, but only
barely. Thankfully, Excalibur was one of the only ships in the system equipped with a
functional jump drive.

When they reached the station, everything became chaos.

Moments blurred together.

Memories overlapped.

Jack only remembered pieces.

He remembered pulling his crewmates into the airlock.

He remembered Valencia's arm.

Half of it was simply... gone.

He remembered the fragments of shrapnel buried in the ballistic glass directly in front of
his command chair. If the fragments had reached him, then they had certainly reached the
rest of the crew.

He remembered the blood.
Too much blood.

More than he had ever seen.

He remembered Marcus.

Six foot five, built like a freight loader, with nearly a foot of jagged metal protruding
from his chest.

He remembered somehow dragging Marcus off the bridge.

He still had no idea how.

He remembered James looking down at the piece of metal sticking through his own leg.

"It doesn't look too bad."

James had pulled it free without another thought.

Then the blood came.

Far too much blood.

James had managed to throw a tourniquet around his own leg before finally collapsing to
the deck.

Jack remembered Bella waiting in Main Commons with medical equipment already laid
out, somehow anticipating exactly what was coming.

He remembered screaming over the comms.

"Bella! Get ready!"

At some point after that...

He docked Excalibur.

Jack honestly couldn't remember doing it.

He didn't remember following procedures.

He didn't remember thinking.

There had been no checklist.

No conscious decisions.
Only instinct.

Training.

Obligation.

He knew how to do it.

The Navy had made sure of that.

He and Valencia had trained together for years.

Emergency casualty recovery.

Battle damage control.

Medical evacuation.

They had practiced scenarios like this countless times.

Just...

Never with people they loved.

This wasn't another crew.

This was family.

Family bleeding across the deck of their home.

The home they had spent the last three years building together.

The thought lingered.

Jack stopped walking.

He found himself sitting on one of the maintenance catwalks overlooking Dry Dock
Three.

Below him, Excalibur hung silently inside the massive repair bay.

She looked broken.

Armor panels had been peeled open.

Scaffolding surrounded the hull.
Engineers crawled over her like ants, cutting away twisted metal and exposing
framework that only days earlier had been hidden beneath pristine armor.

Only a day had passed.

Jack stared at her.

His vision blurred.

Tears slowly ran down his face.

He hadn't cried when they were fighting.

He hadn't cried carrying Marcus.

He hadn't cried dragging James into the airlock.

He hadn't cried while docking the ship.

Now...

With everything finally quiet...

He couldn't stop.

A hand rested gently across his back.

Bella.

She didn't say anything at first.

She simply sat beside him.

Then she pulled him into a hug, resting one hand against the back of his head.

"It's going to be okay, Jack."

Her voice was calm.

"Everybody's going to be okay."

Jack nodded without looking at her.

After a long silence, Bella spoke again.

"I've got something to show you."
Jack wiped at his face.

"I don't think I'm in the mood."

"You are."

There was something different in her voice.

Concern.

The kind that only appeared when Bella had found something she couldn't explain.

She reached into one of her cargo pockets and tossed a small holographic projector onto
the catwalk between them.

A data cartridge followed.

It clicked into place.

The projector came to life.

"I made sure the ship recorded everything," Bella said. "Every camera. Every sensor.
Every subsystem."

A faint smile crossed her face.

"Same thing I did during the alien encounter."

She shrugged.

"Seems to be working out."

Jack looked over at her.

Bella folded her arms.

"I've gone through this recording over a hundred times."

A pause.

"I think I found something."

She looked directly at him.

"I need somebody else to tell me I'm wrong."
The recording began.

The battle unfolded again.

Jack hated every second of it.

Every explosion.

Every alarm.

Every flash of weapons fire.

Every impact.

Every frame dragged him back onto the bridge.

He could almost smell the smoke.

Almost hear Marcus screaming.

Almost feel James collapsing beside him.

His jaw tightened.

Then—

Bella froze the recording.

"Watch."

The video resumed.

One frame.

Two frames.

Three.

Jack leaned closer.

Just before the detached engine nacelle from the enemy cruiser slammed into Excalibur's
bridge...

Something spun through the frame.

Tiny.
Almost impossible to see.

Jack immediately paused the recording.

Bella looked over.

Jack slowly leaned toward the hologram.

"You've got to be fucking kidding me."

James woke slowly.

Everything hurt.

Every movement felt like the hardest thing he had ever done. His body felt drained, as
though every ounce of strength had been pulled out of him. Even opening his eyes took
effort.

The room slowly came into focus.

Bella was sitting beside the bed.

The moment she realized he was awake, she reached over and smacked him on the side
of the head.

"How fucking stupid are you?" she snapped. "Pulling a big-ass piece of metal out of your
leg."

James gave the weakest grin he could manage.

Bella's expression immediately softened.

"I'm glad you pulled through," she said quietly. "It was rough there for a while."

Jack was sitting silently in the corner of the room.

He hadn't said a word.

He had simply been waiting.

James slowly looked around.

The medical room was larger than he remembered.

His own bed sat along the left wall.
Valencia occupied the bed in the center of the room.

Marcus lay to the right.

Marcus was still unconscious.

Doctors and nurses constantly moved around him. Every few hours they wheeled him
back into surgery before eventually returning him to the room again.

James shifted his attention toward Valencia.

She was awake.

Barely.

Her eyes drifted open every few minutes before exhaustion pulled her back under again.

Her left arm was heavily bandaged.

Even beneath the dressing it was obvious how much tissue was missing.

It looked as though something had taken a bite out of her arm.

The doctors had explained what happened.

She had gotten lucky.

Another half inch...

The twenty-millimeter shell that had entered the bridge would have struck the bone
directly, tearing the entire arm away.

If the fuse had functioned inside her body...

There would have been nothing left.

Jack followed James's gaze.

His eyes were red.

He wasn't crying anymore.

Not really.

But it was obvious he had.
James finally spoke.

His voice was barely above a whisper.

"Marcus..."

He swallowed.

"...Valencia."

Bella immediately understood.

She knew that look.

She had seen it before.

It wasn't the concern of a captain.

It was the concern of a father.

She rested a hand gently on the side of his bed.

"Look to your left."

James slowly turned his head.

Bella smiled.

"They're rough..."

A small pause.

"...but they're here."

James let out a slow breath.

The tension left his body all at once.

He closed his eyes.

Within seconds he had slipped back into unconsciousness.

Several days passed.

James drifted in and out.
Sometimes he was awake for only a minute.

Sometimes for an hour.

The doctors assured the crew he would recover.

What surprised them wasn't that he had been injured.

It was that he had survived.

The amount of blood he had lost bordered on the unbelievable.

For a man in his fifties, it was nothing short of remarkable.

The doctors considered it a combination of stubbornness, immediate treatment, and more
luck than any one person deserved.

Thankfully, one thing the Almagest mission had prepared for exceptionally well was
medicine.

Humanity had traveled ten thousand years to an untouched system.

Everyone had understood the risks.

People were going to get hurt.

People were going to die.

The Colonial Authority had planned accordingly.

The hospitals, trauma centers, surgical facilities, and medical research divisions
throughout Almagest rivaled anything humanity had possessed back in Sol.

Bella found herself thinking about that often.

She had helped build parts of this station.

The conduits.

The power systems.

Sections of the medical wing itself.

She had never imagined that one day those same walls would be keeping her family alive.
For the first time since arriving in Almagest, she found herself grateful that she had spent
so many long nights helping build something she hoped would never need to be used.

Now...

It was saving the people she cared about most.

A few weeks later After James was done with his coffee, he walked over to the medical
wing where Marcus and Valencia were staying.

Marcus was still in a coma.

Valencia was out of hers.

She was a real tank.

Apparently all one hundred and twenty pounds of her.

James thought for a second.

I would not want to fight her one on one.

A small chuckle escaped him.

Then he stepped into the room.

Valencia was sitting at a computer, doing paperwork.

Or something important.

Marcus wasn’t there.

James immediately looked concerned.

Valencia looked up from the computer.

She caught the expression on his face and smiled.

“He finally woke up,” she said.

James let out a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding.

“They moved him down to one of the labs so they could check his …something i dont
remember….”

She shook her head.
“That collapsed lung was no joke. Danmm near hit his heart to”

James looked at her, visibly relieved.

“To be fair,” he said, “you had some of your bone missing and a lot of your skin taken off
that arm. And he's lucky to be as big as he is. It saved him.”

He smirked.

“Hopefully the worst part about this whole experience is losing part of your tattoo.”

Valencia looked down at the heavily bandaged arm and let out a small laugh.

“The reason I'm here is because of you,” she said quietly. “So, in some way... that tattoo
being wiped away—or blown away in this case—kind of fits our little family, doesn't it, a
fresh start?”

Humor was always a good resource, James thought.

Humor had a way of bringing a little life into the shittiest situations.

James walked over and looked at the injury with the concern of a father checking on his
daughter.

“Well…”

He nodded.

“That’s gonna be a pretty gnarly scar.”

Valencia shrugged as much as the injury would allow.

“It doesn’t hurt too much anymore.”

She paused.

“At least when I’m not moving.”

Another pause.

“When I’m moving, it hurts a lot.”

James raised an eyebrow.

“So… it always hurts a lot.”
They both smiled.

James looked at her for another moment, walked closer and inspected her more closely.

“Do you need anything else?”

Valencia shook her head.

“All good, Captain.” with a grin

James nodded.

“Good.”

With that, James left the medical wing and started his day.

Not on a positive note, he thought.

But certainly a better one than any day he'd had over the last few months.

As he walked down the corridor, his thoughts drifted back to the day they first met.

Almost absentmindedly, he rubbed the faded Navy tattoo on his own shoulder.

A naval insignia.

The number 54 at its center.

The ship they had served on together.

He had sacrificed his career so Valencia could keep hers.

She had finished her contract.

He never got the chance to finish his.

Yet somehow...

He still had his tattoo.

And she had lost hers.

James couldn't help but shake his head.

Life had a strange sense of humor.
A few weeks passed.

Jack, Valencia, Bella, and James were finally back at the habs.

Life had settled into something almost normal again.

Excalibur would be in dry dock for quite some time. The damage was extensive, and
everyone knew there would be many months before she was ready to fly again.

Now was the time to make home feel a little more like home.

The farmer down the valley had bartered with James for a shipment of animal hides so he
could begin making proper furniture.

Real furniture.

Not the rough things he had been building for years out of scraps of lumber and whatever
wood he could find.

He had picked up woodworking back on Earth, making little tables and cabinets for a
family he had left behind.

Or...

James corrected himself.

A family that had left him behind.

The crew had finished building their own small habs, but nobody was sleeping in them
yet.

Instead, they all stayed together in the first cabin James had built.

It had become home.

Bella spent most of her free time working on the outside of the cabin.

Every now and then she would stop what she was doing just long enough to point out
another one of James's questionable construction decisions.

"You call this craftsmanship?" she asked one afternoon, shaking her head at one of the
support beams.

James shrugged.
"It hasn't fallen down yet."

Bella rolled her eyes.

"That is an incredibly low standard."

"It is a standard."

She couldn't argue with that.

Jack had been quieter than usual.

Far quieter.

The jokes were still there.

Sometimes.

But they came less often now.

James noticed.

This had been Jack's first real combat engagement where the people bleeding beside him
weren't simply fellow sailors or fellow officers.

They were family.

James understood exactly what Jack was going through.

It wasn't James's first time.

It wasn't Bella's.

And it certainly wasn't Valencia's.

She had survived a particularly brutal pirate interception years earlier while still serving
in the Navy alongside Jack.

Combat was never easy.

But fighting beside strangers and fighting beside family were two very different things.

James had expected this.

He knew his crew.
Out on the frontier, surrounded only by the people closest to you, watching one of them
get hurt could feel like the end of the world.

Sometimes...

It was.

Sometimes it happened because someone made a stupid mistake.

Sometimes it happened because everything that could go wrong did.

Sometimes it happened because there simply wasn't anything anyone could have done
differently.

This time...

Everyone had done everything right.

Jack had flown brilliantly.

Valencia had fought brilliantly.

Bella had kept the ship alive.

Marcus had done exactly what he was supposed to do.

James had made every decision he could.

And people had still gotten hurt.

That weighed heavily on Jack.

He was a doer.

He liked fixing things.

Finishing things.

Preventing bad things from happening to other people.

He naturally accepted responsibility, even when it wasn't his to carry.

That was one of the reasons he had become a pilot.

He wanted that responsibility.
He wanted people's lives in his hands.

He wanted to bring them home.

And he had.

He had done a fantastic job.

James knew that.

Hopefully...

One day Jack would know it too.

Because at the end of the day, some things simply happened.

No amount of skill.

No amount of preparation.

No amount of training.

Could change that.

That was life on the Almagest frontier.

Sometimes...

It happened far too often.

Life continued.

Five weeks had passed since Excalibur limped back to the shipyard.

Marcus was still in a coma.

The doctors remained cautiously optimistic.

He was healing.

His body was recovering remarkably well.

Every day the numbers looked a little better.

The swelling had gone down.
The surgeries had become less frequent.

Physically, Marcus was getting stronger.

The problem was that nobody knew when—or if—he would wake up.

The crew visited him often.

Sometimes they talked to him.

Sometimes they simply sat quietly beside his bed.

Nobody knew if he could hear them.

Nobody cared.

He was family.

Family stayed.

Admiral Bishop and Governor Princeton had been more understanding than anyone
expected.

Rather than assigning the crew immediately back to duty, they had given them something
they desperately needed.

Time.

Time to recover.

Time to rebuild.

Time to let their family heal.

For the first time in months, James, Jack, Bella, and Valencia were back at their habs on
Verde.

Working.

Building.

Repairing.

Trying to make life feel normal again.

Valencia had only recently been discharged herself.
Her arm still carried a deep divot where the shell had torn through it.

The muscles had been reconstructed as best the surgeons could manage, but portions of
the damage were simply too severe.

She would require several mechanical muscle replacements before she regained full
strength.

Thankfully, modern medicine had long since solved problems that would have crippled
people back on Earth.

The prognosis was excellent.

With enough therapy and time, she would make a full recovery.

Humans were resilient.

Perhaps more resilient than they had any right to be.

James found himself thinking about that often.

Ten thousand years from home.

A new galaxy.

An alien encounter.

A ship barely held together after a battle it should never have survived.

And somehow...

They were still here.

Still building.

Still laughing.

Still refusing to quit.

Maybe that had always been humanity's greatest strength.

Not intelligence.

Not technology.

Not ships.
Simply the refusal to stay down.

chapters.text:
Admiral Bishop and his ship, Nostromo, were almost permanently parked just outside
the HEI Shipyards.

Not because they needed to be.

The Colonial Authority had plenty of stations and facilities scattered throughout the
system that could have served as a command center.

But the shipyards made sense.

Most of the construction, manufacturing, research, and long-range planning for the
growing colonies flowed through HEI and several larger players.

The shipyard itself had excellent facilities.

Crew accommodations.

Medical bays.

Machine shops.

Fabrication facilities.

Warehouses.

Docking berths.

More importantly, it could comfortably house rotating crews, allowing personnel to cycle
on and off Nostromo without constantly shuttling people across the system.

Over time, the arrangement became less of a temporary convenience and more of a
permanent headquarters.

Anyone looking for Admiral Bishop usually knew exactly where to find him.

If he wasn’t aboard Nostromo, he was probably somewhere inside the HEI Shipyards.
